We illustrate the authenticity of the Whittaker functor within the context of quantum groups. Specifically, we demonstrate that when applied to any finite-dimensional quantum group module, the Authentic Whittaker functor yields a projective module. Notably, by leveraging the quantum affine Schur--Weyl duality, we derive the description that as a $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-module, the image of the authentic Whittaker functor applied to a standard simple module is a direct sum of two finite-dimensional simple modules. This provides an alternative proof of a previously known result. In addition, we describe the image of the authentic Whittaker functor applied to a level-zero module within the Kashiwara--Miki's Fock module realization of the irreducible QPS module. To accomplish this, we introduce a new module structure. (This is a revised version of arXiv:2101.09388)

This paper introduces a new formulation for a broad category of complex optimization problems characterized by uncertain and constrained 'a priori' information, including various types like integer, logical, and combinatorial uncertainties. These conditions are known in advance but not exactly quantifiable, much like unsigned binary integers. To tackle this issue, we developed a Lagrangian dual-based framework for a specific class of such optimizations, including instances like the Stauffer-Wolfe algorithm and Latin square maximum minimum Latin square covering problem. This new approach reformulates the original problem into a more tractable Lagrangian dual form by utilizing available information about feasible solutions, thus allowing for a lower and upper bound on the optimal value to be computed. This method is demonstrated to work efficiently for covering-type problems, including an efficient application to the maximum Latin square covering problem, for which the exact optimal value is calculated with high precision. Finally, we discuss how this method can be applied to a wide range of other combinatorial optimization problems with various types of constraints, including properties like submodularity, supermodularity, and concavity. Moreover, we provide a theoretical proof that our method converges to the optimal solution under specific conditions, including a large enough value for the penalty parameter. This method is successfully applied to a maximum flow problem under uncertain conditions with promising results. Furthermore, we propose an algorithm for a specific combinatorial optimization problem, along with a bound on its computational time. This method is tested and evaluated on an array of covering-type problems, including the maximum Latin square covering problem and others with similar characteristics. To the best of our knowledge, this method provides the first known solution to these problems, including a tight lower bound on their computational times. These findings were validated through numerical experiments, including a maximum flow problem under uncertain conditions, which showed that our method outperforms other approaches like reformulation linearization and cutting plane methods. Our final evaluation and analysis of these results were presented. Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity. For any $R$-algebra $S$, we define a set called $E_R(S)$, consisting of $R$-algebra homomorphisms from $R$ to $S$. The elements of this set can be visualized as 'envelopes' of $S$ within the framework of commutative ring theory. The study of $E_R(S)$ encompasses an examination of their cardinalities. This research aims to investigate the enumerative aspects of $E_R(S)$ and derive a precise formula for its count. Furthermore, it will be demonstrated that this formula represents a unique characteristic, known as an 'enumerative mark', distinct to rings of characteristic $0$. Specific cases and formulas will also be explored, particularly in relation to polynomial rings and dual power series rings. Ultimately, these findings will lead to the identification of marked rings, resulting in new classifications and an interesting paradox involving nilpotent rings of finite enumerative mark in the context of fields. It will also be shown that this phenomenon does not manifest in rings of characteristic $0$. Additionally, some open problems and questions will be proposed to further the advancement of enumerative commutative ring theory. The presented ideas and results are original and have not been previously published. They are an expansion upon the author's master's thesis, which explored the concept of enumerative marks in commutative rings. To improve the efficiency of off-policy deep reinforcement learning using experience replay, we investigate the impact of sampling noise on reinforcement learning performance. A significant drawback of experience replay is likely a side-effect of its design: increasing the variety of experiences at the cost of the accuracy of the target policy, which can hinder the learning process. By modeling the effects of replay sampling noise through covariance analysis, we demonstrate that noise diminishes the effectiveness of optimization methods, particularly when the distribution of rewards is narrow. To mitigate this effect, we introduce a variance-reducing replay scheme that prioritizes accuracy over diversity. Our method employs a time-decreasing bias-variance tradeoff to balance replay diversity and target policy accuracy. The performance of this scheme is evaluated in deep RL scenarios, with results showing improved outcomes compared to standard experience replay in narrow reward distributions and comparable performance in broader distributions. Additionally, the source code for this project has been made available. A thorough empirical exploration of the tradeoff between diversity and accuracy, as well as theoretical considerations of the effects of replay sampling noise on deep RL performance, are also presented in a companion work. Both studies reveal that optimizing parameterization and sampling strategies can significantly impact the performance of off-policy deep RL methods at minimal computational cost. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the intricacies of experience replay and provide a foundation for future research. In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in three dimensions, focusing on solutions that exhibit periodic behavior. Through the use of energy inequalities and simple Fourier space analysis, we derive an analytical bound for the solution in terms of the maximum norm, taking into account initial conditions and non-linear interaction terms. This bound serves as a practical advantage for periodic solutions, differing from the fixed-point theorem's application, which yields a bound tied to the $H^s$ norm by Schauder fixed-point principles. Leveraging this finding, we demonstrate that solutions within the $H^s$ norm's specified range have periodic properties for a finite time period, and also show that solutions meeting certain $\dot{H}^s$ norm criteria are stable over that same time period. Interestingly, the newly derived estimate in $H^s$ norm offers greater sensitivity to initial data than the energy estimate, indicating that small initial data can lead to solutions whose decaying rates differ. Nonetheless, we find that solutions whose growth rates exceed their initial rate will eventually develop singularities in a forward time regime. Using low- and semi-interactive numerical models, we explore the development of these singularities in modelled examples. Ultimately, the results we derive hold for $s$ values ranging from $0$ to $\infty$, serving as a practical and theoretically useful outcome for periodic Navier-Stokes equation solutions. The problem of checking whether a given measurement on some states of a quantum circuit arises from valid physical principles has been solved in superpolynomial time with the emergence of quantum algorithms. However, solving this problem in linear time with respect to the description length of the circuit has been a long-standing challenge. In this paper, a new verification algorithm was proposed that achieves this goal by reducing the problem to checking consistency in a specific set of equations whose size is tied to the circuit's description length. This algorithm is based on a novel reduction to the Maximum Independent Set problem. This study also yields an efficient verification algorithm for verifying applications of a single quantum gate. A related issue of checking whether a given classical probability distribution arises from some measurement of a quantum circuit was also addressed, yielding an algorithm that works in nearly linear time when the circuit's description length is given as input. This issue was resolved for a specific class of circuits (AC^0) over the past few decades; in this work, this resolution was generalized to a broader class of circuits (TC^0). Moreover, a new proof that the unbounded version of the issue can be solved in subexponential time with respect to the circuit's description length was provided, surpassing a prior proof that relied on a different and computationally more expensive problem. A related issue of checking whether a given classical distribution arises from some application of a quantum process (not necessarily unitary) was also addressed, yielding an algorithm that works in nearly linear time with respect to the description length when the issue is given as input. This issue was resolved for a specific class of processes (Clusker-free LOCC) over the past few decades; in this work, this resolution was generalized to a broader class of processes (arbitrarily Clusker-free LOCC). We establish a metric on a Riemann surface, having non-negative uniform curvature and including a finite collection of conical singularities, by adapting Pogoda's method from \cite{Pogoda}, which was initially developed for hyperbolic surfaces. Subsequently, we determine sufficient geometric constraints to ensure the obtained metric achieves positive uniform curvature. Furthermore, we elucidate the relationship between our metric's properties and those of the Weitzenb\"ock cone, which includes all curvature measures. This leads to an interpretation of the cone's curvature via a simple exponential function. As a consequence of our findings, we prove an analogue of Weyl's embedding theorem for surfaces with positive uniform curvature and conical singularities. Additionally, we show that any finite collection of curvature measures can be expressed as the curvature of a specific Weitzenb\"ck cone, thus achieving the optimal order of the cone's singularities' angles. Moreover, we examine the asymptotic behavior of our cone's curvature as the angles approach zero, yielding a first-order Taylor expansion. Finally, through an application of Pogoda's method in the case of positive curvature, we establish Pogoda's result that a surface with finite hyperbolic entropy admits a projective embedding. Furthermore, we derive an analogous result for the case of uniform curvature, providing an alternative proof of the embedding conjecture for embedded compact surfaces with a finite hyperbolic entropy or, equivalently, uniform entropy. 

The methods employed in this study are demonstrated through a variety of examples, highlighting the inherent complexities of controlling the metric's curvature near the singularities. Specifically, we illustrate the divergence of the curvature's behavior from that of hyperbolic metric and that of a surface with a recently introduced bounded curvature metric from \cite{KNT}. This contrast highlights the non-trivial nature of achieving uniform curvature on a surface with a general collection of singularities. We introduce {\sc Flexible Scattering Phenomenology} (${\cal FS}^2$pho), a suite of programs and macros tailored to address phenomenological scattering processes in a flexible and efficient manner. The primary focus is on phenomenology associated with top-quark pair production with high-energy colliders in mind. These include partonic scattering processes, associated distributions, observables, and their corresponding cumulative sums, enabling phenomenological analysis and optimization. The implementation draws on the flexibility provided by FlexTev, a previous initiative. Building on this foundation, we leverage phenomenological distribution parametrizations, effectively constructing a Monte Carlo generator. The resulting ${\calFS}^2$pho program offers a range of output formats and can be integrated with existing programs and generators, including MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO, Sherpa, and Powheg-2.0. This suite of programs and macros serves as a versatile tool for presenting and analyzing scattering phenomenology, particularly useful for phenomenological studies and optimizations in high-energy physics. It facilitates communication between theorists and experimentalists by providing a user-friendly description of scattering processes and their associated distributions. Additionally, it enables rapid generation of phenomenological analysis input, such as partonic phase-space information for {\scHelas} and Pythia-8. 

The paper outlines the underlying scattering phenomenology and its associated concepts and analysis within {\scFS}^2pho, detailing the implementation and providing guidance on its use. Included are discussions of how to utilize the code and verifications of its implementation and stability. Specifically, we provide detailed comparisons with published results and recently developed scattering phenomenology tools, including {\scTwap}. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of numerical integration precision on the cumulative distribution and observe that, generally, increasing precision does not significantly affect the results. Nonetheless, in cases where large systematic uncertainties are present, such as in dilepton dilepton final states, the choice of precision may be crucial. 

This suite of programs and macros complements existing tools and resources for scattering phenomenology and high-energy physics analysis, including FlexTe, FlexDub, FlexGen, FlexFit, {\scTwap}, TopWZ, and the CMS top-quark pair subgroup's phenomenological analysis report.

Recent research in human location tracking privacy has focused on concealing an individual's actual location history by discretizing a Poisson Gaussian conditional prior and treating each node as an independent Markov node. However, previous studies have overlooked the inherent relationships between consecutive locations, which are crucial for understanding personal behavior patterns. This paper presents a novel hybrid location tracking privacy framework that preserves the inherent spatial relationships between consecutive locations by incorporating a Gaussian graphical model with a K-dimensional sparse prior and discrete conditional priors. The framework achieves this by categorizing neighboring locations into K uniform bins and using a sparse prior to determine the transition probability between these bins. The transition graph is learned from a large dataset of normal users, ensuring that the estimated transition probabilities are consistent across individuals. The framework also allows for the accurate recovery of a user's true location history, as demonstrated by empirical results. Furthermore, the framework is evaluated using three real-world datasets: the Stanford Hall dataset, the Mt. MIT dataset, and the Google Mt. dataset. The findings suggest that our approach outperforms existing discretization-based methods in terms of a trade-off between accuracy and privacy, while showcasing the importance of incorporating prior spatial relationships for the accurate recovery of location histories. This paper presents a novel motion planning approach designed for dynamic obstacle environments. The algorithm generates a set of spatially discrete points, each representing a feasible path and incorporating a particular speed. The path network is constructed by iteratively connecting unaccounted for speeds to the already included ones. The viability of connecting two discrete points is determined by checking dynamic collision constraints. When a connection is possible, the two speeds are combined, resulting in the formation of a new polygonal line. Otherwise, the isolated discrete point is added to the network. The process continues until all speeds are incorporated, providing a comprehensive map of all feasible paths. The study also examines the computational complexity of the method, showing it to be dependent on the square root of the number of speeds, independent of the environment's geometric and time parameters. The proposed algorithm has been tested and found to outperform existing planners in terms of computation time. Furthermore, it has been shown that it can generate trajectories with reduced overall planning times faster than random speed approaches. Finally, the method is capable of scaling down speeds to reduce computation time while maintaining comparable results to complete motion planning. The algorithm's performance is evaluated using standard performance metrics to balance planning and execution times. The presented approach is found to be adaptable to diverse trajectories, scalable for various speeds, and efficient in dynamic environments. The results of the experiments confirm its ability to surpass optimal motion planning in terms of execution time while maintaining comparable results. Image features are described using both geometric and radiometric information, and a dual-transformer network is designed to match surfel features across space and time. For efficient processing, image features are compressed into binary codes and stored on the surfel map. When needed, a single-stage descriptor encoder is used to extract new descriptors from test images, enabling rapid image-based localization. The training of neural network-based document ranking models often takes place within a batch-based setting where individual records are drawn at random. Despite this common approach, there remains an issue with sample label noise affecting the model's performance. In this research, we address the concern by implementing bag-level sampling strategies for training, which involves selecting multiple documents at random and assigning them a single label. The model is then trained to predict the weighted average of documents within each bag. Experimental outcomes validate the efficacy of this approach, demonstrating better MRR performance and fewer cases of noisy labels affecting the model's performance when compared to traditional query-based document ranking methods. Moreover, the findings highlight the advantage of bag-level sampling over the standard batch-based setting despite its widespread usage. Interestingly, the proposed method outperforms previously suggested methods for handling label noise under the all-neural model setting. In many real-world applications of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), we encounter difficulties due to restricted access to labeled data. The conventional method of producing high-quality supervisory signals via pseudo-labels often falls short when there are only a few initial labels available. To address this issue, we propose the Informative Pseudo-Tagging (IPT) framework, which incorporates a GNN with a pseudo-tagging module and a memory mechanism. The pseudo-tagging module is designed to generate multiple pseudo-labels per node, taking into account the confidence of the model and the node's neighboring information. The Informed GNN Memory (IGM) then stores these pseudo-labels to provide a rich information context for GNN inference. We conduct various experiments on multiple datasets and find that IPT outperforms existing methods when there are limited labels available. With just 10% labeled data, IPT achieves an average improvement of 4% in edge classification accuracy compared to its best baseline. The source code for IPT is publicly available at https://github.com/whwu1999/Informative-Pseudo-Tagging. IPT has won 1st place in the MSCKG challenge task 2 at NeurIPS 2021. The winning code can be found at https://github.com/whwu1999/MSCKG-MSLR. A family of variational methods based on the optimization of the Kullback-Leibler divergence in a R\'enyi sense is widely used for image restoration. These methods can be further improved by introducing a Tikhonov regularization in their Proximal gradient optimization. We show that the resulting regularized optimization problem is equivalent to the balanced energy minimization of the sum of the original log-contrast function, a Tikhonov regularization term, and a boundary penalty function. To solve this problem, we develop a proximal gradient algorithm as a starting point and establish its convergence for exponential R\'enyi divergence. We also provide numerical evidence that our approach can outperform current state-of-the-art methods in terms of image denoising. Finally, we demonstrate the potential of our method for solving sparse reconstruction problems by experimenting with data from MRI. Our method performs favorably in comparison to previously used techniques. A comprehensive mathematical framework for our method is provided in a previously published work (Bonnabel et al., 2020), and our numerical experiments for regularized R\'enyi divergence optimization presented in this study. This study examines how primordial black holes can originate from the oscillations of a curvaton that's less massive than the inflaton. Unlike traditional models, where primordial black holes form as a result of inflaton fluctuations, in this case, the curvaton's oscillations lead to an early matter-dominated period, causing primordial black holes to form during this stage. By incorporating a variation of the quintessence model, we find that a suitable model exists that not only generates a correct abundance of primordial black holes but also affects the inflationary background in a noticeable manner, resulting in a slight deviation of the primordial power spectrum from flatness, with a magnitude that's easily detectable. This model is characterized by a self-correcting behavior, with a very weak dependence on the model's parameters, making it highly testable. Additionally, we find that while some of the parameters may require further refinement to be fully consistent with observations, the abundance of primordial black holes in this case aligns with both astrophysical data and theoretical predictions, serving as a complementary understanding of this phenomenon. Overall, we find this model to be both compelling and robust, offering a fresh perspective on the formation of primordial black holes. As such, it presents an exciting opportunity to explore this topic further, both theoretically and experimentally. Furthermore, we outline the prospects for experimentally verifying this model through a combination of ground-based observations and space-borne investigations, including the search for the cosmic microwave background spectrum and gravitational waves produced by primordial black holes. The extensive use of real-time large-scale radio interferometers in contemporary astrophysical data collection necessitates a calibration approach that can process data at a rate of N channels per 10 microseconds, with a computational complexity of logarithmic orders. Our research proposes a novel calibration technique that can achieve this data rate. This method calculates antenna phasings based on the properties of discrete exponential functions and can be performed efficiently using the Fast Fourier Transform algorithm for a regular grid layout of antennas. With this approach, we can derive a set of independent equations that can be solved using FFT's logarithmic-order scaling. Our initial tests using simulated data approximately doubled the computational time compared to traditional single-pixel calibration methods. Nevertheless, we have also developed an optimized algorithm with an O(N log N) scaling that we can apply directly to real data. Our optimization strategy involves rearranging the calculation order of the equations and using techniques to reduce data copying, thereby yielding a significant 70% reduction in computational time. Our algorithm with this improvement is now capable of calving hundreds of channels in under a millisecond and has a scalability limit of over 2000 channels. Our final tested method involves a calibration time of approximately 830 milliseconds for 2024 channels. We believe this method has the potential to greatly contribute to the development of real-time large-scale radio interferometers. Our code for this method is available for public use and has been successfully applied in the construction of the Hi-C spectrometer. We present a novel, autoencoding conditional Generative Adversarial Network model that effectively diversifies portfolio distributions. Next, our GAN trainer instructs a generator to create new, more diversified portfolios in a training data space with reduced dimensions. It has the added benefit of being easy to use, as it requires no prior knowledge of either machine learning or finance. In clinical trials for Alzheimer's and progressive diseases tracked with continuous data, the augmented Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic is used to compare distributions, which is particularly significant as it doesn't violate assumptions. A problem with this approach is that it doesn't utilize all gathered data, which can result in reduced statistical power. To rectify this issue, a novel method using natural cubic splines is introduced, designed to examine statistical differences in continuous data distributions in Alzheimer's clinical trials. This method is compared to the augmented Kolmogorov-Smirnov approach through simulations and practical application. The results indicate that the new method yields improved statistical power with comparable p-value distributions. A case study involving the CRESENT trial is also conducted to illustrate the usefulness of this approach in evaluating treatment effects. The statistical analysis from this case study suggests no substantial treatment effects were found for patients receiving solanezumab or lanadelumab in comparison to the placebo, which was consistent across multiple comparisons including the novel method, the augmented Kolmogorov-Smirnov approach, and other conventional analyses. This paper's primary focus is on the theoretical identification of standard functions within typed lambda-calculi, but it also includes a significant practical aspect in its concluding section. We explore the effects of different degree distributions in a model of inhibitory neurons using a type-I intensity-based model. Building on past work by Melillo et al., who analyzed an analogous model with a power-law degree distribution, we examine networks with various distributions, including a narrow, Gaussian degree distribution and multiple others derived from the stabilization parameter gamma. For gamma less than or equal to one, we identify a neuronal population that inhibits synaptic inhibition, while larger values of gamma enable the emergence of bistability, including oscillatory states. As gamma increases, the neuronal population transitioning to spiking activity expands, with a limiting case that mimics a complete network of inhibitory neurons. For gamma greater than or equal to two, the dynamics converge to a state where neurons fire in a regular, synchronized pattern. Furthermore, we establish that the neuronal population that spiking activity emerges from is determined by the degree distribution, with a secondary stability transition occurring for gamma greater than one. For gamma greater than two, the system exhibits a transition to a synchronized state with a uniform inter-spike interval. For the degree distributions derived from gamma less than one, we observe oscillatory states, while larger values of gamma lead to synchronized states with a uniform inter-spike interval. For gamma equal to two, the system exhibits a transition to a synchronized state with a distinct, finite inter-spike interval. Moreover, we observe that the system exhibits a transition to a synchronized state with a uniform inter-spike interval as gamma increases beyond two. These findings highlight the intricate balance between neuronal connectivity and dynamics, emphasizing the significance of considering the structure of neural networks. The analysis also provides insights into the mechanisms governing neuronal behavior, including the interplay between local inhibitory processes and global synchronization phenomena. Such insights are crucial for addressing the complexities of neural systems and designing neural circuits. The presented model serves as a versatile tool, encompassing a wide range of degree distributions, thereby facilitating the systematic exploration of neural synchronization in inhibitory networks. As such, our analysis is relevant to various neural systems, including those found in cortex, ganglia, and retinal processing. The system's behavior is also reminiscent of experimental observations in epilepsy, microstrip and superconducting quantum circuits. Moreover, our findings are particularly significant in the context of artificial neural networks and systems, where inhibitory neurons are essential for competitive mechanisms, and synchronization is crucial for information processing. Finally, our model is also applicable to biological systems, including the case of Staphylococcus aureus bacterial colonies where inhibitory interactions prevent competitive mechanisms

In this context, we introduce an adversarial training technique that strikes a balance between data utility and privacy preservation. This method employs an adversarial trainer to safeguard patient data while allowing the disease prediction model to learn from the transformed data. Our proposed approach is capable of transforming raw medical data into a secure, encoded format for use in learning tasks, thereby ensuring data privacy while enabling accurate disease prediction. The goal of this study is to investigate spatial patterns in homicide rates in Goias, Brazil from 2002 to 2014, with a focus on discovering recurring patterns in temporal and spatial data. To achieve this, we applied the Lee, Tung, and Chen algorithm to create a time-varying map of homicide rates, which enabled us to identify and analyze clusters at different levels, including state, municipality, and polysgmaic (combined) areas. Our analysis revealed the presence of four types of clusters: municipalities with high homicide rates, state-wide, and multiple smaller-scale clusters. By examining these clusters, we were able to understand the varied geographical and temporal distribution of homicide rates and identify potential non-uniform patterns in official law enforcement data. Furthermore, we were able to use these insights to make inferences about the underlying causes of homicide, such as the presence of a heroin epidemic and the impact of election-related policies, which could inform more targeted and effective interventions. To the best of our knowledge, this study represents the first attempt to apply the Lee, Tung, and Chen methodology to aggregate level data in Goias, Brazil. Stochastic gradient descent is a widely used optimization algorithm in machine learning, particularly in situations where access to gradient information is limited. The algorithm has well-documented convergence properties when operating within a bounded function domain, but these properties rely heavily on the presence of stochastic noise. When encountering rare, unusually large outliers, the algorithm can experience significant slowdown, despite having little insight into the origin of such events. In an effort to create a more robust stochastic gradient descent algorithm, we investigate its behavior in the presence of noisy data. This study examines how the algorithm's performance correlates with noise characteristics and outlier frequency, drawing on previous work which established its asymptotic convergence under varying noise conditions. A more detailed understanding of this relationship is then created through the development of a probabilistic model that incorporates all relevant parameters. This model reveals a crucial insight: that stochastic gradient descent is sensitive to outliers, but resilient to noisy data. Building on this insight, we propose a novel stochastic gradient descent algorithm that automatically adapts to data conditions. The algorithm is shown to be either accelerated when operating within a stable noise environment or robust against outliers, thereby achieving optimal performance in diverse data configurations. Numerical experiments conducted across multiple domains demonstrate that the proposed algorithm is capable of achieving a balance between stability and efficiency. The corresponding code has been made available for further research purposes. Ultimately, this work provides essential groundwork for the development of future adaptive optimization techniques in machine learning, and potential applications are explored in the conclusion. This work addresses online platforms, which act as intermediaries between service providers and clients, and aims to maximize the income from these platforms. The total income is represented as a sum of clients' and providers' earnings. To optimize the system, we investigate the exchange of service quantities between clients and providers as a T-T game, which can be classified as a Tu-Paradox. By applying Tu-Paradox characteristics to this scenario, we prove that our game is implementable as a Tu-Paradox. By converting this game into a standard convex optimization problem with the properties of a regular function, we can apply the Convergence of Bregman Iteration algorithm to show that data exchange between clients and providers converges to a stable state, which ensures the system's optimality under the presence of these intermediaries. By removing the intermediaries, we investigated a scenario in which clients directly purchase services from providers under a given pricing mechanism and found the stable state that ensures the system's optimality under Bertrand pricing. Moreover, we proved that our algorithm to maximize income under the presence of intermediaries is applicable to the case of Bertrand pricing with or without these intermediaries. By applying the Charnes-Cooper transformation to our optimization model, we can reformulate our model as a conic optimization problem that can be efficiently solved using the interior-point method. By numerical testing, we have shown that our optimization model effectively increases online platform income under both scenarios with or without these intermediaries. Finally, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of our model through the testing of real-world data on online job platforms. 

Keywords: Online platforms, intermediaries, T-T game, Tu-Paradox, implementation, convergence, optimality, Bertrand pricing, interior-point method, real-world data, online job platforms.

To create abstractive summaries, we can use an existing summarization model as a 'teacher' to guide a smaller'student' model, which can then replicate the teacher's performance based on provided examples. Typically, this involves the teacher generating summaries from a set of source documents, which are then used to train the student model through supervised learning. However, pre-collecting these teaching examples can be resource-intensive and may not always be applicable to new domains due to changes in language usage. To address this, we developed an approach where the teacher and student models work together in a planning process to create new examples of summaries, which are then used to train the student. This example creation process is based on goals defined by the planner, which are derived from the teacher's summary. We found this approach to be effective across two datasets and multiple domains, as it led to improved summarization performance when compared to traditional methods of pre-collecting examples and fine-tuning the student model alone. Importantly, this progress can be achieved through relatively simple and efficient planning processes that do not require complex optimization problems to solve. We also noted that the teacher models we developed produced summaries that were very similar to those generated by large pre-trained language models used for conditional generation, which may be worth exploring further in the future. This research was conducted as part of a new GEC dataset collection that addresses gaps in existing work and data shortages in the field. The findings presented here have significant implications for the development of methods for zero-shot and few-shot learning for abstractive summarization models. They also highlight the importance of improving pre-trained models' ability to generate coherent and meaningful summaries, which remains a pressing issue in NLP at the time of writing. Further details about the research, including the data collection process, are available in the accompanying document. To facilitate future advancements, we have made our code publicly available. As of now, our code has received over 200 unique views from researchers. Further research could involve extending the findings presented here to other applications of natural language processing. One potential area for further study could be the development of methods for weak supervision to create high-quality training examples for natural language understanding using NLP. This could involve a similar approach to the one presented here and leveraging the findings to improve model performance on key NLP tasks. Moreover, our research has relevance to the emerging field of document-level NLP, as well as several key NLP challenges and competitions, including the 2020 TAC KBP and the 2019 NLP Summit

This research presents new sufficient conditions for differentiating a function with n real variables, where these conditions are grounded in the differentiability of a related function with n-1 variables and are less restrictive than traditional criteria. We have derived these results while addressing a specific problem that had been posed by the Spanish Academy of Language. The findings were also used to establish differentiability criteria for n complex variables under similar conditions applied to their real counterparts. The theoretical work has been applied to various applications, including the determination of the exact values of the first distributional derivatives for specific n-variable polynomials that are relevant in computer vision and the creation of new interpolation methods for n-dimensional data sets. The procedures used to prove the results can be automated. The research has been conducted with the primary objective of establishing a mathematical framework for the tasks of interpolation and data reconstruction. The methods developed align with the principles of least-squares and superleast-squares. The data sets employed in the experiments consist of points on polynomials and on the surface of an n-dimensional hypercube. The exact solutions to the interpolation problem for 2-dimensional vectors have been obtained by generalizing a method that was originally designed for 1-dimensional interpolation. The generalization was based on a convolution approach. The specific solutions for the interpolation of values on an n-dimensional hypercube were obtained by combining a convolution-based method with the approximation of the convolution function through a (n-1)-variable function, which had previously been derived in another research project. The research was conducted in the context of a doctoral thesis and the resulting data sets for the experiments have been made available on GitHub. The procedures used in the research have been executed using the programming languages Julia and Python. The research was conducted between 2018 and 2020. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. In contrast, $v_3$ from hadronic collisions shows a strong correlation with the initial geometry's triangular component, albeit only for central collisions. The reasons behind this correlation were also explored. Our findings indicate that the triangular flow component $v_3$ is largely influenced by pre-equilibrium dynamics rather than hadronic collisions. As a result, $v_3$ from hadronic collisions tends to be less correlated with the initial geometry in more central collisions. Additionally, the study found that incorporating a triaxial equation of state can potentially strengthen the correlation between $v_3$ and the initial geometry's triangular component. Future experiments at various collision energies are expected to verify these conclusions. The study further highlights the importance of distinguishing between flow contributions from pre-equilibrium dynamics and hadronic collisions, particularly when interpreting experimental data. The exponential growth in automotive sensors is producing an immense amount of data, primarily consisting of visual information. This data is being used in advanced technologies, including adaptive cruise control and self-parking systems. Edge Computing is bringing computations closer to the data's source, leveraging Stradling's Law to optimize processing by shifting tasks between Edge and Cloud resources. This paper proposes a framework that utilizes contributions from participating vehicles to execute computations on the Edge, while considering factors such as privacy and byzantine resilience. This framework addresses two key issues: 1) creating a secure and efficient method for distributing data and weight updates, and 2) developing an robust and efficient aggregation method that preserves accuracy despite the presence of malicious actors. This approach is evaluated using the FullNet framework, which allows for a comprehensive analysis of our method's performance. Our experiments show that the proposed framework achieves high accuracy, even in the presence of up to 50% malicious activity. This performance is comparable to that of centralized architectures, with the additional benefit of increased byzantine resistance when the number of malicious actors exceeds 20% of the network. This research provides an in-depth examination of the challenges and solutions within Edge Intelligence in the automotive sector, while offering a potential solution to address privacy concerns in Edge Computing. We introduce a concept called Euler characteristic universality, which is defined as non-trivial solutions to an equation involving the Euler characteristic and a fixed functional, and investigate their characteristics. Such universality equations originate from diverse fields including classical mechanics, optimal control, fluid dynamics, electrical engineering, gravity theory, and cosmology. A notable example is the Hill type operator, which is central to optimal control theory and variational mechanics. We examine the existence and countability of universality solutions from a functional analytical perspective, and explore their topological properties, while also highlighting their distinct periodicity patterns arising from different functional scenarios. Moreover, by employing Birkhoff-Green operator theory and Bethe-Sommerfield formula framework, we establish a systematic approach to quantitatively calculate the Euler characteristic functional, and discuss its various generalizations, including the product-Euler characteristic functional, product-Bethe-Sommerfield formula, and extended Birkhoff-Green operator theory. Our work also contributes to revisiting the Polyakov action from a novel functional perspective and revises the formula for the n-th order Euler characteristic of a compact Riemann surface. We further generalize the results to two-dimensional conformal maps and the Gaussian free field on compact Riemann surfaces. In addition, we show that the extended Birkhoff-Green operator has applications in computing the Euler characteristic of an ordinary differential equation system and provide an intuitive understanding of the non-trivial universality solutions as well-as-youthful states of dynamical systems. We also discuss their relation with entropy and sibylline prophesies. Lastly, we explore the implications of the universality functional being an invariant under a conformal map, and investigate its properties in the context of conformal field theory and quantum gravity. A key outcome of this investigation is the discovery that the conformal invariance of the Euler characteristic universality equation leads to a crucial result, which is a product-Bethe-Sommerfield formula. We also generalize this result to a formula for the n-th order Euler characteristic of a compact Riemann surface, and establish its applications in computing the Euler characteristic of a conformal map. Therefore, the current research primarily focuses on the analytical and topological properties of the universality functional, whereas its dynamical and controlled aspects are explored in detail under specific functional scenarios. Our recent studies of the effects of Rh content in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ reveal the emergence of magnetic irreversibilities and spin freezing in the vicinity of x ≈ 0.6, accompanied by a suppression of long-range ferromagnetism. Through detailed analysis of the temperature and field histories, we observed distinctive depolarization behavior across the relevant Rh content range. Specifically, for Rh contents below x ≈ 0.6, the materials exhibit standard ferromagnetism with a Brillouin wall contribution during temperature increases. Conversely, for Rh contents above x ≈ 0.6, the materials display a pre-ferromagnetic state with spin freezing instead, and further increases in Rh content result in a complete suppression of long-range ordering and gradual replacement by a spin glass phase. Moreover, our findings for Rh contents above x ≈ 0.6 show a reversal of the Brillouin wall contribution under external fields – now occurring during temperature decreases. This phenomenon can be attributed to a competition between Ce $f$-electron-mediated and Rh $5d$-mediated Kondo interactions, leading to spin freezing at the critical Rh content of approximately 0.60. Our results provide conclusive evidence of spin freezing using high-field neutron depolarization, thereby offering a unique perspective on the competing interactions within these heavily mixed anisotropic ferromagnets. Furthermore, we propose that similar mechanisms may be operational in other Ce, Pr, and U systems exhibiting spin-glass, antiferromagnetic, and ferromagnetic behaviors upon doping. Ultimately, our research highlights the utility of high-field neutron depolarization as a sensitive tool for uncovering subtle magnetic phenomena in complex systems. The recently proposed Legendre Memory Unit is a type of recurrent neural network that employs a unique memory mechanism based on the properties of Legendre polynomials. This paper examines the computational aspects of LMUs, demonstrating a parallel training algorithm that can be implemented using standard GPU infrastructure. Additionally, experiments were conducted to optimize the training process of LMUs. Results show that training parallelized LMUs on modern GPUs yields significant speed improvements, achieving a $35$ times faster training time compared to CPU-based methods. With the aid of batch normalization, even faster training times were attained, specifically about $42$ hours for a full $10$-hour CPU benchmark on a GPU such as the Titan X. This substantial acceleration enables extensive network hyperparameter combinations to be tested and evaluated in a relatively short period of time. Furthermore, the optimized training protocol enabled the collection of a comprehensive dataset for reproducing key LMU performance metrics. This dataset is publicly available on the related GitHub repository. Several network architecture modifications were proposed, including one that yields an improved LMU variant, dubbed the 'parallelized-OMZU,' which achieves a $0.7\%$ enhancement in the MNIST benchmark compared to the original OMZU. This variant also exhibits a $6$ times faster training time, surpassing the speed of various competing RNN memory networks, including the Long Short-Term Memory model. In particular, the parallelized-OMZU outperforms other competing models: it reaches an $85.3$ accuracy on MNIST with $10$ hours of CPU training, whereas the competing models reach at most $84.7$ accuracy with extensive CPU training. However, some of the competing models reach higher accuracy on CIFAR-10, specifically VanHatten $84.819\pm 0.006$, LSTM $83.519\pm 0.006$ and wide-resnet $83.906\pm 0.006$. Interestingly, the parallelized-OMZU also demonstrates a $7$ times improvement in the N-MNIST benchmark compared to the OMZU. This variant also outperforms other competing models on the N-MNIST NCM and NVM benchmarks. Results also indicate that the parallelized-OMZU generalizes better to the N-MNIST NC and NV benchmarks compared to the OMZU. Formal verification offers precise assurance, but writing specifications in a formal language can be a burden on specification authors and may alienate those without expertise in that language.  This could be eased if programs could be based on natural language specifications, but translating English descriptions into a predicate logic language without losing their meaning is a complex problem.  This is because English descriptions often imply facts beyond what is directly stated, and weakening the implication risks invalidating the specification.  This project explores whether it is possible to write verified programs based on logical forms of natural language specifications, and how close we can get to allowing program developers to write programs based on English descriptions, without necessarily requiring expertise in formal languages.

As a first step, we have developed a proof system that allows reasoning about programs based on predicate logic specifications.  This project involves defining rules for deriving specifications that must be satisfied by programs, and demonstrating that these rules preserve program correctness.  This proof system serves as a foundation for developing algorithms that translate specifications from logical forms to Hoare logic, enabling the verification of programs based on natural language specifications.

Although our proof system supports a significant range of programs with loops and conditional statements, it does not cover programs with procedures, and certain features like early returns from loops.  This limitation is due to difficulties in deriving specifications that must be satisfied by programs from specifications that describe their local behavior.  This project also addresses the challenge of specifying programs from logical forms, and proposes a method for doing so, as well as demonstrating its applicability to a range of programs that must be shown correct.

Finally, we have applied this proof system to verify a range of programs that write their local Hoare logic specifications as a result of translating natural language descriptions.  This involves defining algorithms that translate logical forms to Hoare logic specifications, and demonstrating their applicability to programs with loops and conditional statements.  These results bring us one step closer to allowing program developers to write programs based on English descriptions, and specification authors to specify programs based on logical forms without losing their meaning. 

Related projects have addressed specification inference and verification, but this project differs in its focus on specifying programs based on their Hoare logic specifications, and translating natural language descriptions to logical forms to enable this specification.  These projects specify programs without pre-defined specifications, but this project specifies programs based on pre-defined specifications that describe their local behavior.  These projects also address specification and program verification, but this project specifies programs that write their local Hoare logic specifications as a result of translating natural language descriptions.

This paper proposes an innovative method called BayesOD, fusing the precision of modern object detection focus and the uncertainty estimation capabilities of Bayesian learning. Utilizing a variational inference technique and the mean-field variational approximation method, BayesOD assigns a structured uncertainty distribution to each component convolutional filter in the detector's network, enabling accurate estimation through a two-step latent variable introduction method. This approach not only enhances performance, but also allows for the quantification of uncertainty during training. Through comprehensive experiments on standard test datasets including ImageNet, COCO, and VOC, BayesOD demonstrates superior performance with stable and quantifiable uncertainty estimations. This problem has been extensively researched, and a key concept is the most tap set of a vertex, which represents the minimum number of taps required to reach it. Determining whether a vertex's most tap set equals the number of vertices in the graph is a challenging problem, and we investigate this issue by focusing on graphs known as "edge-critical" bipartite graphs. In these graphs, adding an edge increases the minimum number of vertices required to return all vertices to their original state. We show that if an edge is present in these graphs, it's possible to verify in linear time whether the vertex's most tap set equals the number of vertices in the graph or not. Furthermore, in the case of bipartite chordal graphs, this problem can be solved in linear time as well. These findings extend previous research, and they reveal a connection to flow-disjoint vertex pair problems that was previously identified. To optimize analysis precision while managing acceptable computation time, there's a trade-off between reaching the absolute limit and a satisfactory approximation in Abstract Interpretation. The balance between these is a continuous challenge in Abstract Interpretation, a problem we address by re-examining the fundamental principles of this theory. Traditional Abstract Interpretation frameworks necessarily follow a single upward trajectory, interpreting programs one step at a time, with no opportunity to reverse course. We propose a new theoretical framework that enables a two-way analysis, where a program's execution can be temporarily reversed. This flexibility allows distinct phases in the analysis: an initial upward phase to establish initial bounds and a subsequent downward phase for refinement. By decoupling these phases, the optimal precision-time axis ratio can be more easily determined. We also introduce an abstract domain for Pin-based systems that facilitates a cost-effective transition between phases. Furthermore, our experimental results demonstrate that using a two-way analysis can achieve a seven-fold improvement in precision for the same time investment. The accompanying tool can be accessed at https://bitbucket.org/sergioxrc/dacp. The core analysis described in this thesis has also been implemented as an Latticed-based Abstract Domain within the Astre\`o verification platform, available at https://astree.verification.com. With this implementation, our numerical evaluation of Astre\`o's domains, encompassing over 200 programs, shows that a two-way analysis yields, on average, six times more precise abstract invariants in comparison to the traditional one-way approach. The optimal precision-time axis ratio in Astre\`o's one-way analysis is thus reached six times faster with our proposed two-way analysis. This additional geometric insight empowers analysts to make an informed choice between precision and efficiency, striking an ideal balance between the two. The interaction between a two-level atom and a one-dimensional quantum Einstein cavity, modeled as a massless scalar field and a perfectly reflecting mirror, is studied using stochastic quantum Brownian motion. When the atom and the Einstein cavity are in a thermal bath at temperature $T$, the atom's jump correlations are influenced by stimulation due to its own movement. It's found that the stochastic differential equation for the atom's vector state $\mathbf{r}(t)$ contains a stochastic potential resulting from the radiation of electromagnetic and scalar fields. This potential depends on the probability of spontaneous emission $Q$, the mirror's presence, and the atom's coupling parameters. For $Q=1$, the electromagnetic field correlations are found to be non-Markovian, continuous, and low-frequency, resembling the behavior of underdamped Brownian motion. This is reflected in the asymptotic scale-invariant radiation behavior of a faceless atom, where energy is conserved: the electromagnetic and scalar potentials become time-invariant and spatially homogeneous. However, when the atom and the Einstein cavity are in contact, the system forms a non-linear system of coupled mean field equations. Two stable steady-state solutions are present: the radiation of a faceless atom and a frozen, entangled $|{LS=2;m_s=\pm 1}|$ state with zero temperature bath. This is due to the mirror's reflective properties preventing energy exchange between the atom and the Einstein cavity. It's also observed that spontaneous emission below the critical distance of $|{k r=1.43}$ prevents the system from reaching the radiation stability of a faceless atom. This is similar to the Casimir-Polder force dipole approximation where energy exchange between the atom and the Einstein cavity is not conserved. The system is also shown to have a non-equilibrium steady state with a time-dependent, low-frequency asymptotic scale-invariant radiation behavior when the critical distance is broken. This is due to the mirror's reflective properties and the atom's finite probability of spontaneous emission. The system's behavior can potentially be observed in experiments with ultra-cold atoms using optical mirrors. This is because the required radiation bandwidth can be achieved with sufficiently long relaxation times and large radiation gaps. For example, this can be done with a 786 nm wavelength optical balloon or a 100 nm wavelength optical grating used in ultra-cold atom experiments. At balloon-balloon distances of 10-100 micrometers, the required low-frequency asymptotic scale-invariant radiation behavior can be observed before spontaneous emission occurs.

However, showing all reviews to users may lead to information overload, and displaying a small, randomly selected set of reviews may not cater to their individual interests. This paper addresses this challenge by proposing a Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN) that learns to recommend reviews in a personalized, relevance-sensitive manner. This approach involves two key components: 1) an interactive generator that uses a user-specific model to select reviews, and 2) a fusion network that combines review features to create a comprehensive and engaging set. This method also considers review sentiment in the review-centered recommendation process. Empirical evaluations on two real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of SIFN in improving both task completion rates and average ratings compared to baseline models. In social situations, agents can achieve more by working together and adapting to each other's actions than by acting independently.  Often, the best way for two agents to cooperate is for one to initiate the interaction, waiting for the other to respond.  This can create a problem because the agent that starts is unlikely to encounter many opportunities for the other to respond, resulting in it becoming stuck in a state where it doesn't receive the desired actions from its partner.  This is known as the 'initiator problem', and it has been found to occur in a variety of applications including multi-agent collaboration and learning.  A new algorithm, transfer empowerment, has been developed to address the initiator problem by leveraging the agent that starts to create opportunities for the other to respond, using a novel approach that encourages variability in its actions.  This leads to a significant increase in the agent's ability to provoke the desired actions from its partner, resulting in improved cooperation.  A multi-agent learning and collaboration context, building on prior research in learning to coordinate, found that the algorithm, transfer empowerment, and a combination with an established technique for increasing action variability, maximum entropy reinforcement learning, and a novel reinforcement learning approach, resulting in improved cooperation and learning through self-improvement.  The research and findings are expected to have a significant and positive impact on a variety of applications including the 'initiator problem', and it is anticipated that the algorithm, transfer empowerment, and its associated theories and models, may be widely applicable to a variety of domains and problems.  A future work has been suggested which could expand upon prior research in the field. In the field of solar physics, a widely used technique for estimating the solar vector magnetic field has been developed, although it comes with a limitation of potentially biased data. A new approach, known as assessment bias, has been introduced to describe the systematic errors associated with this technique. In an effort to correct these errors, various correction methods have been proposed. In this study, different types of bias are defined and distinguished, and a comprehensive evaluation is conducted to assess the effectiveness of multiple correction methods in a controlled environment. Von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem exhibits varying convergence rates based on the type of spectral gap in a compact abelian group. The difference arises from the choice between using discrete Fourier analysis, which records frequencies without amplitude, and periodization, which records frequencies along with their multiplicities. The comparison is drawn through a metric space with specific metrics that account for the scale of frequencies, showing that the convergence rates are effectively measured in this scale. The analysis also provides an example where the rates can distinguish between distinguishable sequences, but a power-law rate fails to distinguish it in a limiting case, and shows how this non-distinguishable case shares properties with equilibrium states of quantum dynamics where measurements yield partial observables rather than exclusive valuations. The conclusion includes consideration of ergodicity and measurements in quantum systems. The mathematical analysis relies on tools like Weyl sums and the methods of Harman (2011) and Montgomery--Van der Corput (1935), which estimate these sums. The most rapid known rates for Fourier analysis and periodization share a common structure, but the innermost argument of Weyl, as given in Harman (2011), is insufficient for proving the outer part of periodization by equivalent methods. The periodization result is instead proven using a combination of Harman's methods and van der Corput's results, which also help address limit cases and distinguishable sequences. The distinction between the results is further solidified by considering Steiner ratios in geometric heuristics. The analysis also includes consideration of observables in the context of von Neumann algebras using a similar distinction in a context from Tomita--Takesaki theory. The conclusion includes consideration of observables and the measurement problem in quantum systems. The work includes an appendix on Lebesgue summation, a fundamental concept in integration theory, and includes an additional consideration on distinguished sequences in probability theory.

We employ a corpus-based approach using metadata such as word count, syllable count, and word frequency. Leveraging Bayesian model selection, we discover that languages with greater morphological complexity, characterized by longer syllable sequences and skewered word frequency distributions, are more likely to incorporate non-alphabetic scripts. We find a positive correlation between syllable count and word frequency distribution, but not when syllable count is instead correlated with phoneme count. We suggest that syllable count serves as a proxy for morphological complexity, while word frequency distribution reflects syntactic complexity. Finally, we find that phoneme count influences syllable count. Our findings are validated by cross-linguistic comparison. We explain the discrepancy in syllable length through the influence of phoneme count. Our results imply that languages with non-alphabetic scripts tend to have increased morphological complexity. To explore this concept, a study has developed a method to simulate the collapse of self-interacting dark matter in small-scale gravitational lensing events within galaxy clusters that have mass less than $5 \times 10^{14} M_{\odot}$. These simulations, conducted using the GADGET-2 code, have focused on small-scale lensing between galaxies in the Coma and M49 clusters, based on actual observations. To better understand the results, two types of self-interacting dark matter models are used, each with different collision cross-sections depending on the velocity of the particles involved. These simulations show that collision cross-sections less than or around $10^{-3} \, \mathrm{m}^{2} \, \mathrm{kg}^{-1}$ are consistent with observed lensing data, including both strong and weak lensing effects. Additionally, the study found that small values of the collision cross-section can naturally account for the lack of satellite galaxies in certain clusters without requiring significant collision cross-sections to explain this phenomenon. Overall, the study's results support the idea that self-interacting dark matter is a plausible candidate for gravitational interactions in galaxy clusters. We examine the challenge of lessening Markov Decision Process models based on limited visibility into the system's behavior. In this study, we explore the utility of partial observations derived from randomized insight into the polices being evaluated. To distinguish our method from existing traditional partial-obs model simplification techniques, we have developed a novel approach called partial-obs randomized simplification. This technique yields a generalization of the exact reduction method when used with definitive observations, thus making it comparable to established methods. Notably, our technique produces a reduction that is free from optimization problems, making it applicable in situations where the polynomial-time and NP-hard cases differ slightly. We have also shown that the technique can be extended to handle cases where there are multiple, non-contradictory partial observations. This extension allows for the simplification of value functions using multiple, non-contradictory partial observations. To address the challenge of learning these partial observations, we have developed an optimization-based algorithm that iteratively uses them to simplify the MDP model. This algorithm first applies partial-obs randomized simplification to generate new, non-contradictory partial observations for the next iteration. Experimental results show that this algorithm is effective in finding simplifications even when starting from a single, non-contradictory partial observation. Additionally, it outperforms traditional methods when given only a set of non-contradictory partial observations. This algorithm is also versatile, as it can be used with MDPs, POMDPs, and MDPs with unknown rewards or transition functions. To facilitate its use, we have developed a tool that automatically translates standard MDP format to a format that is usable for simplification. This tool is available for download at http://cse.uta.edu/~ruchir/pos.html. Further details on the technique and its implementation are provided in the author's thesis at http://www.uta.edu/ecs/dissertations/. This algorithm is implemented in C++ and distributed under the terms of the MIT License. To encourage its use, we have also created a simple graphical user interface using Qt that is also distributed under the MIT License. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/ruchir/pos. This project is maintained at https://github.com/ruchir/pos. The authors can be contacted at ruchir@cse.uta.edu or http://cse.uta.edu/~ruchir. A prevalent method, Autoencoders, is widely accepted but the original framework is somewhat rigid, restricting exploration of novel techniques. An advanced method, Autonomous Component Analysis (ACA), has been introduced as an enhancement to traditional Deep Autoencoders, employing a two-stage process - construction and selection. Within the ACA framework, the selection stage is subjected to constraints, which often leads to the non-applicability of the ACA method under certain circumstances. To address these limitations, we present M-ar-K-Fast ACA, a modified ACA method where the selection stage is replaced by a single, integrated process. By merging the two steps, the non-applicability issue is resolved and the method becomes more adaptable, allowing incorporation of the autonomy principle and handling diverse manifold challenges. Spreading social media information helps people stay informed about events, but it also generates massive amounts of data that researchers must sift through to uncover what's new. To address this, we developed a system using Twitter data that automatically identifies emerging trends based on user-generated content and can pinpoint where incidents are unfolding in real-time. By combining geotagged tweets with statistical modeling, we track and monitor the spread of events, and leverage data analysis for research and investigation purposes. Our system, called Incipio, consists of multiple components, including an algorithm that detects anomalies in data and identifies clusters of related tweets, all running on an open source architecture for improved accessibility. By showcasing its capabilities during the 2019 Sri Lanka bombings and the 2020 Halloween wildfires in California, we demonstrate Incipio's effectiveness in identifying new events and tracking their progression across space and time. Ultimately, our system serves as a resource for researchers and investigators to use as a starting point for in-depth explorations into social media conversations. Our system is available for public use at https://github.com/kipr1/incipio. With its open-source nature, we hope that other researchers and investigators can build upon what we've created and contribute back to the community with their own innovations. These alloys are part of a larger family of compounds that can be synthesized with varying cobalt concentrations. By searching this composition space, this paper uses an evolutionary algorithm to find new cobalt-rich compounds with superior thermodynamic properties, such as lower $\Delta H$ values for H absorption and desorption. The algorithm identified four new cobalt-rich compounds with lower $\Delta H$ values for H absorption and desorption, including a unique phase with a higher H absorption capacity and lower $\Delta H$ values for H desorption compared to existing phases in the Y-Co-B system. These newly discovered compounds have potential as cobalt-free replacements in the YCo$_{11}$ and YCo$_{19}$ alloys, reducing their cobalt content and mitigating concerns over cobalt toxicity. The cobalt-rich compounds in the Y-Co-B system can be used as an effective search strategy for cobalt-based hydrogen storage compounds. By incorporating cobalt into existing phase families, researchers can discover new cobalt-rich compounds with improved H absorption properties. This strategy can also be applied to other phase families to discover new hydrogen storage materials. A crucial phase in quantum key distribution (QKD) involves privacy amplification, which consolidates the generated keys into a single, highly secure key. Prior studies on the security analysis of QKD have typically overlooked a critical factor - the source of random seeds in this process. In reality, these seeds are rarely truly random and may exhibit non-uniformity, which could significantly impact the security of the final keys. To address this gap, we introduce a new method for analyzing the security of QKD, incorporating the effect of non-uniformly generated random seeds on the privacy amplification step. By developing a unified security analysis framework, we demonstrate that this new method can achieve comparable levels of security as traditional approaches, even with a single source of non-uniform randomness. Furthermore, our experimental results validate the practice of using a single, moderately high-quality random seed source for privacy amplification, without compromising the final key's security. This research provides valuable guidance for practical quantum measurement implementations, where true randomness sources may be scarce. In particular, it offers crucial insights for field tests of QKD, where dealers may encounter non-uniform random seeds due to using low-quality random number generators. Our analysis bridges the security analysis gap for QKD and quantum measurement, highlighting the importance of random seed quality in these applications. Ultimately, we hope that our findings inspire further research on the intersection of information theory and randomness, with significant practical implications. Our approach also paves the way for extending our analysis to other information-theoretically fundamental problems. To establish trust and ensure fairness, algorithms used for making critical decisions must be transparent and understandable to those impacted.  Although there is no single established framework for measuring algorithmic interpretability, we develop a novel framework that quantifies interpretability in relation to human learning.  This framework consists of a cognitive complexity score (CCS) and a learning difficulty measure (LDM) that increase in tandem with the complexity of the task at hand.  By applying this framework, we test the interpretability of various algorithms used for making categorical predictions, including different versions of logistic regression.  This framework not only assesses algorithmic interpretability but also provides a measurable standard for human learning, thus offering a new perspective on the relationship between human cognition and algorithmic transparency. This study examines the effects of temporary shocks on permanent outcomes in an impulse response function framework. It shows that in cases where there are dynamic interactions between variables, local projections may not adequately capture these relationships. To address this issue, the study proposes a flexible local projection model that improves impulse response function estimates. A Bayesian information criterion is used to select the most effective lag structures for each outcome variable, leading to the development of a flexible local projection model. Simulation results reveal that this model outperforms traditional approaches such as AR models in estimating high-order impulse responses. Additionally, the study applies the model to analyze the fiscal multiplier in South Korea and finds that a sudden increase in government spending leads to sustained increases in government revenue. It also reveals that a sudden economic contraction in the US is followed by a sustained decline in Korean imports from the US. Furthermore, the study finds that a sudden US economic decline leads to a significant decline in Korean economic growth through a channel involving imports from the US. Overall, the study provides novel insights into the dynamics between the US and Korea through these impulse response estimates. These results highlight the utility of the flexible local projection model in practical policy settings. To our knowledge, this study is the first to adapt the local projection model to estimate complex dynamic relationships. A Monte Carlo simulation shows that the proposed model outperforms alternative models such as AR models in estimating high-order impulse responses. A Bayesian approach to model selection is found to improve the accuracy of these estimates. A key contribution of this study is the practical application of these theoretical models to real-world data. It is expected that these results will be of interest to policymakers in both the US and Korea. To facilitate replication, we provide a detailed description of our methods and data, as well as the associated code using zypackage. A copy of our manuscript can be found at https://goo.gl/5f6nr9. A key finding of our study is that the US economic recovery following the 2008 financial crisis was slower than the recovery in Korea, prompting a comparison of the dynamics between the US and Korea. To better capture these differences, we consider the cases of sudden improvement and decline. These results are obtained by applying the flexible local projection model to data from the OECD. A key finding is that a sudden improvement in the Korean economy, as observed following the 2008 financial crisis, is followed by a sustained increase in the stochastic process. Conversely, a sudden decline in the US economy during the 2008 financial crisis is followed by a sustained decline in the stochastic process.

Recent advancements in deep learning have yielded impressive performance in coarse-grained named entity recognition tasks, but research has been lacking in the pursuit of more precise entity recognition with refined subcategories. To address this, we present a new approach called FGNET-RH, which achieves fine-grained named entity identification by leveraging a hierarchical neural network that refines entity representations in hyperbolic space. This approach not only enhances entity representation through a hierarchical structure but also improves classification performance using refined classes. As far as we are aware, no existing dataset for fine-grained named entity recognition has been established, so we generate the FGNET-RH dataset through a semi-automatic process, and the results indicate that this dataset contains 15 distinct subcategories within the PERSON category. We then develop a new model, FGNET-RH, which achieves state-of-the-art performance in both coarse and fine-grained named entity recognition tasks on various neural network architectures. This model is based on a hierarchical self-organizing map, and it refines entity representations through a multi-task learning framework.
