To gauge the level of engagement in conversations, an entrainment metric is needed, one that adjusts according to the similarities in speech characteristics that participants exhibit. Through the application of a Deep Neural Network (DNN) to data derived from the Switchboard corpus, an unsupervised model has been developed, capable of identifying instances of entrainment without requiring explicit labels. By training the DNN to minimize the differences between participants' speech patterns, especially their pitch and energy, it's possible to assess the extent to which their voices converge. As the quantity of available corpora is generally limited, a technique called Data Augmentation (DA) is introduced, allowing for larger, artificially enlarged datasets to train the model. Furthermore, DA facilitates the comparison of similar groups, such as non-native speakers, enabling analysis of their potential for entrainment. By evaluating the model using both the Mean Average Precision and the Normalized Mutual Information (NMI), it's possible to achieve high precision and specificity of over 90%. As a result, it's feasible to create a real-time entrainment detection system, with implications for its use in fields such as HR management. Future plans include expanding the model to recognize synchrony, an essential aspect of entrainment assessment, and examining the limitations of modeling entrainment from native and non-native speakers. Additionally, it's essential to conduct a more thorough analysis of the model's potential biases. Future goals also involve creating a practical application of this entrainment model, for instance by automating a process in HR management to identify highly entrained individuals who demonstrate natural conversation abilities despite being non-native speakers. Moreover, it's possible to apply this model to other fields, like educational settings where understanding between teachers and students can benefit from entrainment detection. Finally, future objectives involve developing real-time applications for entrainment detection, such as live video conferencing services where live entrainment prediction could facilitate smoother interactions.

We show that when the labels from the target domain are revealed at test time, domain adaptation can be transformed into a hypothesis adaptation problem across the parameter space. We name this hypothesis shift and present a semi-supervised approach to tackle this adaptation by utilizing unlabeled target data and the labeled source distribution. We represent the adaptation goal as solving a bi-objective optimization problem: maximizing source performance while also matching the target distribution. To solve this, we develop a two-stage training method that first finds an optimal target network and then performs domain-invariant feature learning. We evaluate our approach on two challenging adaptation scenarios, across five different domains, and achieve a notable average improvement of 9.9% compared to the top existing methods. The code and models are available at https://github.com/ConfusedCar/SSHSFA. We also conduct an ablation study to further understand the performance contributions of unlabeled target data and label regularization. Furthermore, we provide insights on the role of distribution alignment and the characteristics of successful adaptation across the studied adaptation scenarios. Lastly, we discuss potential future research directions based on these findings. We observe that when the adaptation scenario is known in advance, the source domain can often be matched to a synthetic domain through trivial data processing, rendering domain adaptation unnecessary in certain cases. We also note that when the adaptation scenario is unknown in advance, the model must learn to adapt across the adaptation space on its own, without prior knowledge of the scenario. We speculate that incorporating prior knowledge of the possible scenarios could lead to better adaptation outcomes. We also speculate that training multiple models to adapt across different scenarios could lead to better adaptation outcomes. The potential scenarios could be represented as a latent variable that can be learned from the data, through autoencoding the target labels, to provide a better prior understanding of the possible scenarios. We also speculate that using unlabeled data from the possible scenarios for unsupervised learning could further improve adaptation outcomes. We also speculate that training the model to minimize the entropy of the adaptation space could lead to better adaptation outcomes. We also speculate that training the model to learn a common representation across the adaptation space could lead to better adaptation outcomes. We also speculate that training the model to transfer knowledge from one scenario to another under constraints could lead to better adaptation outcomes

Initially, existing nuclear GCE designs were reviewed, followed by a description of particle fuelbed evolution during combustion within a rocket engine. Subsequent sections explore combustion dynamics, fluid dynamics, and heat transfer in rocket engines, culminating in a discussion of the respective models and numerical tools developed for analyzing GCEs. This is followed by a detailed examination of the various methods for propellant management in GCEs, including active, passive, and inert systems. Finally, a summary of the findings from one-dimensional numerical simulations of the respective models is presented, with a discussion of the merits and limitations of each approach for nuclear GCEs in the context of propellant management in low gravity environments. Additionally, a comprehensive list of available resources and contact information for relevant areas of research has been compiled and is presented at the end of the report. Overall, a comprehensive and systematic analysis of the various components and processes in GCEs has been undertaken, with a view to identifying the key challenges and opportunities for leveraging these systems in the development of propulsion technologies for deep space missions. In experiments where multiple astrophysical particles collide, determining the precise point of collision is a crucial objective. A novel deep learning technique utilizes a specially designed layer to map high-dimensional data into a target area, without the need for a complex grid-based structure. This approach is illustrated through its application in two distinct scenarios, where it is used to position collisions within a disk-shaped and spherical volume. Furthermore, a variant of this method is demonstrated to be optimal in identifying particle collisions within a thin disk-shaped area near the Earth's surface, where it was observed to offer a significant improvement over existing models, with a gain in log-likelihood of up to five orders of magnitude. This technique is particularly relevant to experiments such as LOFAR, where it can be used to analyze particle collisions occurring on the surface of the Earth in a two-dimensional structure. Additionally, a neural network model is presented that can position particle collisions occurring on a spherical surface, where it was observed to yield results comparable to a recently proposed method. However, the model for the spherical surface is found to be more computationally intensive than the technique applied to the two-dimensional structure, where the additional parameters required by the former are largely compensated for by the use of a broader range of input data points. To facilitate the understanding of these models, a comprehensive analysis, including key source code components, is provided in accompanying notebooks, where they can be executed to produce the results described in the report. Ultimately, the technique is seen to be versatile, with its ability to be applied to a wide range of curved surfaces, from simple 2-D structures to complex 3-D volumes. However, the deeper input structure is found to be more suitable for the simpler 2-D case, whereas the shallower model is found to yield better results for the more complex 3-D case. Analysis of the models is further explored through their application to simulated datasets, where it was found that a significant proportion of data points are required for the deep network to reach its optimal performance. This is in contrast to the less deep model, which is found to be more resilient to variations in the number of input data points. Despite the models' ability to efficiently position particle collisions across a wide range of astrophysical surfaces, their potential sources of bias are found to be significant, with the need for a more in-depth analysis of these factors being identified as a key area for further investigation. To facilitate this investigation, a variety of analytical models are presented, which can be used to help identify and quantify sources of bias in the models

The presence of continuum opacities in astronomical atmospheres is primarily due to molecular absorption, and accurate treatment of this absorption requires consideration of various vibrational and rotational states. Given the vast number of possible state combinations, direct calculation becomes impractically resource-intensive, and typically, data for relevant molecules is obtained from tables precomputed via line-by-line integrals. However, these tables often lack essential features such as temperature dependencies and rotational broadening. To address this issue, we have developed a novel approach and associated database, EXOPLINES, specifically tailored for studying the atmospheres of brown dwarfs and giant exoplanets. This framework encompasses key absorption molecules, including water, ammonia, methane, and carbon dioxide, and provides comprehensive cross-sections for 77 distinct molecular species, encompassing up to 3125 vibration-rotation bands. Our work is described in a published paper, and the EXOPLINES data archive can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.737643. Additionally, a low-level Fortran library is provided, enabling users to rapidly and efficiently apply molecular cross-sections to diverse atmospheric scenarios. As such, EXOPLINES is designed to facilitate the efficient modeling and simulation of various celestial bodies' atmospheres. Furthermore, a related Python package, PyEXOPLINES, is available for dynamic usage within Python scripts and atmospheric radiative transfer codes. This package can be accessed at https://github.com/astro-antsyrima/PyEXOPLINES. By providing molecular absorption data with precomputed broadening on the Zenodo platform and as open-source software, respectively, we aim to enhance the transparency and reproducibility of associated research outcomes. As a result, the models utilizing EXOPLINES data can produce accurate results, and the code within PyEXOPLINES can be flexibly adjusted to suit the specific needs of various projects. This novel infrastructure is expected to significantly contribute to the existing model spectra and radiative transfer codes, and due to its open nature, it is anticipated to significantly impact the field of study, and the code will continue to evolve to address emerging spectroscopic challenges. We address the challenge of conditional inference in a non-fixed multivariate time series with unknown parameters by first using a heavy-tailed linear model to create a representation of the data, and then applying a Bayesian approach to a simplified, low-dimensional representation for unconditional and to a linear model for conditional inference. Our method yields consistent estimations for the critical parameters of a Scott model that encompasses heavy-tailed behavior. A thorough simulation reveals that our inference procedure is robust, incorporating benefits from the two representations - though it's clear that the first one is required for estimation and uncertainty quantification. Furthermore, we apply our method to the analysis of financial time series, specifically in the study of event analysis and tail dependence investigation, demonstrating our inference procedure's effectiveness. The distance-$r$ dominating set problem, where the goal is to remove a subset of vertices from a graph to make it possible for each vertex to be reached by a shortest path from at most $r$ remaining vertices, has a more tractable variant called the distributed distance-$r$ dominating group problem in the context of networks. Here, a set of vertices that form a dominating group under a given partition of the graph are those that, under a specific distribution, ensure every vertex in the graph has a shortest path to at most $r$ vertices within the group. In this paper, we explore distributed distance-$r$ dominating groups on sparse graphs with a high girth. It is demonstrated that constructing a distributed distance-$r$ dominating group on such graphs is feasible, although the efficiency of this task depends on the parameter $r$. Specifically, for a given integer $r$, we show that a distributed distance-$r$ dominating group can be constructed in near-linear time, effectively determining a dominating group in near-linear time as well. Conversely, for a fixed value of $r$, we find that the task of constructing an optimal distributed distance-$r$ dominating group on sparse graphs with a high girth is computationally tractable, taking at most polynomial time to solve. Furthermore, in the non-optimal case, for a distributed distance-$r$ dominating group on sparse graphs with a high girth, we find that the task of constructing such a group in near-linear time is also feasible. In addition, in the context of distributed computing, for a partition of a graph with a high girth, we find that the task of computing a distributed distance-$r$ dominating group in near-linear time is also feasible, where the computational load per vertex can be made as small as $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$, where $n$ is the number of vertices in the graph. Recent advancements in neural rendering have shown promising results for generating realistic images of unknown environments, but most methods rely on additional lighting information or an accurate lighting model. Our new approach to neural rendering system learns to accurately render 3D scenes using only a single unlit image and an off-the-shelf lighting model, making it particularly suitable for applications requiring real-time rendering. By leveraging a versatile forward model that accounts for various lighting effects, our approach can be universally applied to a wide range of scenes types. Our system has been successfully tested on multiple datasets and shown superior performance compared to existing methods, rendering 3D scenes with similar accuracy to those using additional lighting data. Our implementation details, including code and model weights, are available at https://bit.ly/bfnr. Additionally, our approach enables various interactive applications such as generating novel views, transforming 3D shapes and adjusting materials and lighting conditions. Observations conducted at the SOAR telescope in 2021 along with previously unpublished data, yielded a substantial dataset of 1735 measurements across 1288 pairs and 1177 targets. A significant discovery of this study includes identifying 54 novel pairs or subsystems among nearby dwarf stars, primarily, adding to our ongoing speckle program. Our speckle program aims to monitor orbital movements of binaries within the solar neighborhood, specifically, to establish or reaffirm the existence of 25 such binaries. Furthermore, our analysis provided or reinforced orbital period data for 8 more binaries, with some resulting in changes to their period values. On the other hand, our speckle program also helped categorize 8 pairs or sub-systems, previously classified as extrasolar, where new or revised data was obtained including HATS-11 bc, with the latter resulting in a resolved separation of 0.5588 arcseconds. Additionally, our analysis provided or reinforced orbital period data for 7 more extrasolar sub-systems, with one notable result including a resolved separation of 0.6527 arcseconds for M5+M4 at WDS 17355. 

It's worth noting that our dataset also includes 1177 targets, with a significant number being Hipparcos candidates for possible members of moving groups such as AFT, UGE, and TUC, where further research is needed. These research goals include 1) determining the level to which binary characteristics influence movement patterns, 2) establishing whether binary parallax data can accurately predict group membership, 3) comparing the effect of binary and non-binary stars on parallax measurement, with the latter resulting in a notable -0.0317'' difference in parallax measurement between binaries and solitary stars. 

Lastly, our dataset also includes 1177 targets, with a significant number being non-binary stars at distances beyond 100pc, where further research is needed to determine the level to which binary characteristics influence stellar parameters, with the binary/non-binary distinction resulting in a notable 9.94x10^-4 magnitude difference in V band.

A comprehensive analysis has been conducted to evaluate the compatibility of the two Higgs doublet model with multiple observational indicators, including discrepancies related to lepton flavour universality, a muon magnetic moment, and neutrino oscillation data. Considering a general approach by allowing all model parameters to vary freely, a global $\chi^2$ has been determined and compared with its SM equivalent. With the SM as a reference point, we find that the $\Delta\chi^2$ value is $6.4\sigma$ for $B$-meson anomalies and $3.4\sigma$ for the muon magnetic moment when combining all experimental limits. Additionally, various scenario projections have been examined, including the possibility of observing deviations from the SM at the high luminosity LHC and future neutrino experiments. Furthermore, corresponding predictions for Higgs boson coupling modifications have been obtained and will be made publicly available for use within the Higgs Working Group of the LHC. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the two Higgs doublet model is capable of addressing several observational indicators, albeit failing to significantly contribute to the search for new physics indicators. Consequently, the two Higgs doublet model is capable of providing a long-term explanation for multiple observational indicators, potentially serving as a long-term new physics frontier beyond the SM. The concept of quantum entanglement is fundamental to quantum information and has been observed in the photon number distribution of twisted photons in boson sampling experiments. However, the field of study has been limited to this single aspect, leaving uncertainty about the entanglement present in the complete quantum state. Our work addresses this gap, introducing a theoretical model that applies the principle of von Neumann entropy to demonstrate entanglement in twisted photon states, where the states are represented by number-raising operators of different Twisted Photon Number (TPN) modes. The presence of entanglement in these states was confirmed across all TPN modes and demonstrated to be robust against loss, even when one photon is absent, thereby meeting the criteria for genuine entanglement. The findings have significant implications, suggesting that the non-classical behavior exhibited in boson sampling should be attributed to the presence of entanglement within the quantum system as a whole, rather than relying solely on coherence. This conclusion has far-reaching applications, challenging existing theories of TPF modes and revealing new opportunities for theoretical and experimental research in this field. Our study provides a framework for the analysis of entanglement in multi-mode twisted photon states and their potential use in boson sampling. The research has been further developed to demonstrate the non-locality of TPF modes by applying the principles of Bell inequality and Leggett-Garg inequality. Moreover, the study identifies TPF modes of 3, 4, and 5 TPN as exceptional cases that are resistant to quantum interference and introduces the concept of quasi-classical behavior, where the entanglement of these states is attributed to a unique combination of coherence and entanglement. The findings have been validated by numerical simulations using quantum entropy estimation algorithms. The study also identifies the entanglement of TPF modes of 6 and more TPN as sensitive to quantum interference and challenges existing theories of TPF modes of 3, 4, and 5 TPN by attributing their behavior to a unique mixture of coherent and entangled configurations. In various fields of life sciences, researchers analyze temporal sequences to 
extract critical insights into organism processes such as gene expression, 
metabolism, and cell development. These sequences are often brief, multidimensional 
and contain missing values, making them challenging to work with. Existing methods 
are limited as they often compromise on precision, ignore relationships between 
sequential data points, or inadequately handle missing values, making them unsuitable 
for diverse temporal sequence analysis applications. We introduce a new deep 
learning approach, capable of efficiently learning from and accurately identifying 
temporal sequence patterns in high-dimensional, short-length data with missing values. 
This novel model is uniquely positioned as it the first to tackle this specific 
challenge and can handle up to 8 inputs per step. We demonstrate our approach's 
efficacy by successfully identifying cell state transitions in single-cell time-course 
gene expression data. This approach's open-source code and supporting data can be 
accessed at https://github.com/zhengwuxu/gnet. We also provide pre-trained models for 
download at https://www.dropbox.com/sh/2q3j9gq1x0x0x0x/AAAABT4x4x0x0x/zip?ttl=30d.

Reinforcement learning agents that interact with partially observable environments rely on utilizing information resources, which may involve using attention or specialized oracles to access relevant data. From the perspective of the agent, these information sources can be regarded as additional internal observations that originate from hidden states closely tied to optimal decision-making beliefs. These hidden states function as a form of 'black box,' offering the most valuable information available. In this study, we explore whether recurrent neural networks can serve as an adaptation of this 'black box' model, enabling hidden states to convey a grasp of the inner workings of partially observable environments. Using a simplified scenario, we found that recurrent neural networks can identify and communicate the hidden states necessary for making informed decisions in partially observable environments. Our results also indicate that these networks can self-correct and adapt when information about their 'black box' is gradually made available. When we applied this model to more complex scenarios, such as a grid-world scenario, our results showed that agent performance could be significantly improved if the hidden states of their 'black box' were accurately represented. This finding suggests that utilizing internal observations from specialized information sources as additional observations can greatly benefit reinforcement learning agents operating in partially observable environments. It also sheds light on the similarities and differences between the 'black box' model and recurrent neural networks, providing potential explanations for these results. From a theoretical perspective, our study provides insights into the characteristics of hidden states required for optimal decision-making in partially observable environments. It also highlights potential avenues for further research, such as investigating whether 'black box' models can be learned through reinforcement learning, and whether other types of internal observations can lead to similar improvements, especially when environmental observability is adjustable. In addition to these theoretical contributions, our study provides a practical approach for enhancing the performance of reinforcement learning agents operating in partially observable environments by incorporating specialized information sources as additional observations. Such a technique has significant implications for a wide range of real-world applications where agents often interact with partially observable environments. It also has potential applications in fields such as robotics, computer gaming, and computational biology. Implementation details, including code and data, are available online at the authors' website. In terms of computational complexity, our study provides a practical approach for improving the performance of reinforcement learning agents operating in partially observable environments. It also sheds light on the scalability of our technique, especially when applied to highly complex scenarios. In particular, we found that utilizing specialized information sources as additional observations can greatly benefit reinforcement learning agents operating in moderately complex scenarios, such as the grid-world scenario used in our study

Current data structures for approximate membership query filters, which aim to reduce the likelihood of false positive matches, do not consider the cases where a query might not match any data in the collection at all. This paper proposes a new approach, using a specific data structure called SKIPP, which ensures there are no false positive matches when a query is posed. A thorough empirical comparison of SKIPP has been conducted against four established AMQF algorithms on a variety of collections, demonstrating its performance benefits. Experimentally, the results indicate that on average, SKIPP achieves a 5.6x factor for large collections and a 42.2x factor for collections of size 100, outperforming the other methods by at least 1.4x and 6.8x respectively. Furthermore, the study found that the optimal threshold for minimizing false positives, while also avoiding false negatives, often does not exist in many cases. This highlights an essential requirement for a new approach: the necessity of a data structure that combines the properties of a set filter and an range filter to effectively address this issue. Based on this understanding, the development of a new structure, called ActivePartitionFilter, was initiated. As shown in the study, the APF surpasses SKIPP's performance, reducing the average number of false positives by at least 5.0x and 7.1x, respectively. Subsequent improvements to APF led to its final iteration, called ActivePartitionFilterOptimized, which exhibits superior performance in comparison to SKIPP, averaging at least 2x better. Moreover, the results indicate that APFOP outperforms the best existing filter - PlusP - while also achieving performance comparable to or better than loading the actual set into a hash table for various collections, depending on the size and number of data points. Ultimately, the results of the study indicate that APFOP sets a new benchmark in achieving balanced performance. Following further optimization, the final version of APFOP was introduced, which outperforms all existing algorithms, achieving up to a 100% improvement in performance, while also achieving an average of 85% and 59% less false positives compared to PlusP and SKIPP, respectively. This current version of the algorithm will be used in further evaluations and comparisons. In addition, the study provides valuable insights and recommendations for future advancements in achieving optimal performance at various data sizes. Moreover, the study provides essential guidelines for experimentation design and analysis of new algorithms and data structures. Finally, the study results in a valuable resource

We introduce an enhanced method within Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) that enables modeling distinct fluid properties using a single simulation, by incorporating pressure and viscosity as separable physical attributes. This formulation aligns with thermodynamic principles and leverages the use of higher-order and anisotropic SPH kernels for more accurate simulations. The presented method is exemplified by simulating multi-component flow and fluid-structure interactions where particles can transition between being solid or fluid based on dynamic pressure and viscosity conditions. This is exemplified through various multi-component simulations at different resolutions, including monolithic and multi-particle scenarios, as well as fluid-structure interactions, including coupling with rigid bodies and thin-shells. Comparisons with High-Fidelity simulations reveal the SPH framework's accuracy and robustness in simulating both single- and multi-component systems. This is implemented within the framework of the SPHin3D code, an open-source SPH library. A compact VQ-Wav2Len model, named FastPitch, was presented for pitch transformation and speech synthesis. Although it efficiently handles large-scale datasets, its pitch modification capabilities are limited. A new, improved approach called pitch augmentation has been introduced, allowing for more natural and controllable pitch variations. The enhanced system uses an auxiliary module to preserve timbre during the training process, ensuring that FastPitch maps the same embedding to different pitches while maintaining distinct timbres. Results from zero-pitch and forgeries testing reveal that pitch augmentation yields more natural and human-identifiable speech when the same text is spoken with different pitches. Furthermore, the integrated system allows for semi-supervised learning, enabling more natural and controllable pitch transformations in languages with reduced dataset sizes. Subsequent experiments on English and Portuguese demonstrate the success of this method. Moreover, the proposed system outperforms comparable state-of-the-art approaches in both language synthesis and pitch transformation tasks. A user study on Portuguese demonstrates that the augmented system produces high-quality and natural speech that surpasses commercial standards in terms of speech quality and authenticity. This paper focuses on two key research questions and provides an in-depth analysis. It details an experimental drive scenario where 20 users controlled a robot remotely through a latency-variable network and rated its performance. These users also completed a separate sound-quality experiment. This implies that interactive quality is best assessed through a combination of physical and cognitive aspects. This paper will focus on BHLMs as a solution for various Bayesian regression models, discussing their application in missing data estimation, nonparametric induction, and classification tasks. This paper aims to provide an accessible introduction to BHLMs, along with practical examples and methodologies for implementing them, with a particular emphasis on practical applications and considerations. Deep convolutional neural networks with large kernel sizes have demonstrated the ability to compete with or surpass performance of smaller kernel models at a reduced computational cost. However, standard mixture-of-experts architectures with parallel expert networks and a router that assigns inputs to experts face limitations in this context. The underlying reason for this is that a router with a limited number of outputs cannot adequately distinguish between inputs when the number of experts increases, especially in cases where the kernel size of each expert is large. To overcome this limitation, we developed a new type of router that integrates with an alternating direction of data partitioning and expert retraining. By dividing data into smaller subsets and assigning them to individual experts for further refinement, the proposed router can effectively handle a large number of experts. Our method was shown to consistently outperform benchmark models with small kernel sizes on various tasks and even compete with large kernel size models that were previously considered optimal. Moreover, our method was found to be computationally efficient in terms of inference time and parameters. Finally, a thorough investigation of the method's properties through a strong theoretical foundation was provided. By exploring the chip-firing game on genus g curves with hypercanical tails, we can determine the genus of a binary Jacobian, identify its Jacobian counterpart, and describe its holomorphic 1-forms in relation to its Jacobian's degree. This theory is further applied to classify binary Jacobians of genus g with a degree 2g. Additionally, we will discuss the classification of primitive binary Pryms of genus g and degree 2g for some special cases. This theory also reveals a natural connection between the chip-firing game's contact invertibility group and the Torelli group, which shares many overlapping invariants in the study of genus g curves with primitive Jacobians or Pryms. Ultimately, this theory allows us to classify binary Jacobians of genus g with a degree g+1 everywhere and a special self-intersection -g of a particular arithmetically coherent effective divisor, which is also known as half-canonical tails. This classification is achieved by exploring the chip-firing game on genus g curves with these particular half-canonical tails. Here, the theory is used to classify binary Jacobians of genus 2 and degree 4, and binary Pryms of genus 3 with a degree 5 for some special cases. The management of applications across varied multi-cloud and on-premise environments poses significant challenges due to the complexity of interactions between applications, services, and infrastructure. Many existing tools are inflexible, often focusing on specific technologies or offering features not essential to general deployment needs. To address these challenges, a new container approach called Ozy was developed. Currently available open-source solutions, such as Kubernetes, focus on scaling applications across multiple resources, but Ozy was designed to simplify infrastructure management by standardizing operations across multiple cloud and on-premise platforms. Unlike other approaches, Ozy was built from scratch with a focus on universal applicability, feature modularity, and a simplified architecture. Many features, such as high availability, can be enabled by default, but also allow users to customize and choose only what they need. Ozy was successfully tested in multiple cloud and on-premise platforms, including Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, AliCloud, and on-premise environments. Additionally, a demonstration of Ozy's features was given at the 2022 Open Source in Cloud (OSC) conference. Our evaluation shows that Ozy outperforms Kubernetes in terms of resource usage, with Ozy using 10% fewer CPU and memory resources across all tested platforms. We believe that Ozy's unique design makes it a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners looking to simplify and standardize multi-cloud and on-premise infrastructure management. Our analysis, based on scenarios involving 1000 customers and 2000 requests, demonstrates that the Branch-and-Cut method can find optimal solutions within 1% of optimal in under 1 minute, even with very strict time limits. Furthermore, model tightness allows for the Branch-and-Cut method to find optimal solutions up to 20% of the time compared to loose formulations. This study examines the relationships among several information-theoretic measures of complexity in Boltzmann machines, which are neural networks consisting of fully connected layers. To assess the optimal state complexity of BMs and the effects of learning on their information measures, a BM with 5 x 5 binary units was trained and simulated in various setups. One group of simulations fixed the weights while introducing noise, demonstrating a decline in state complexity. Another group, which allowed weights to be adjusted through stochastic gradient descent and included an 'inertia' factor to stabilize the learning process, revealed correlations among the information measures, with the exception of average mutual information, which did not demonstrate significant relationships. These findings suggest that the structure of BMs is best evaluated using measures of structure complexity, which capture the interconnections among units, while the optimal state configuration of BMs is best understood through measures of state complexity. Ultimately, our results indicate that the optimal state complexity of BMs should be minimized when generating efficient representations, which can be achieved by maintaining an optimal balance between the complexity of the model and the learning process. By simultaneously minimizing the structure and state complexities of BMs through an optimal balance of 'organization' and 'entropy', it is possible to achieve a stable BM state with predictive power. Interestingly, our data reveal that the information measures exhibit correlations even in the presence of conceptual ambiguities, which is evident in the 'dogness' attribute - measuring how 'doggy' a pattern is - that was introduced into the BM. To translate speech into written text, speech recognition systems initially convert speech into a sequence of words, and then modify the words to match the sounds and context of the given sentence.  One critical step in this process is inverse text normalization (ITN), which corrects any word spacing or letter modifications induced during the transcription.  Since ITN is usually performed separately for each word, researchers typically create an inventory of common words and associated normalization rules.  Nevertheless, numerous uncommon words in languages cannot be covered by this approach.  In contrast, deep learning methods have proven to be effective for uncommon word ITN despite the limited availability of corresponding training data.  In this study, we employed a sequence-to-sequence model with a self-attention mechanism to tackle unseen words in languages.  In order to compile a dataset for this model, we proposed a data augmentation method by combining two types of artificial data generation.  In addition to standard training data, we created pseudo data by applying a word-level model to standard training data, and then combined it with another word-level model that used pseudo ITN training data. We examine the application of neural networks for processing the word embedding model, Word2Vec, to identify key phrases in a given text. To achieve efficient processing on IoT devices, we investigate whether reducing the vocabulary size of the embedded words from 30 million to 20,000 affects the network's ability to accurately predict key phrases. Our findings reveal that a Word2Vec network with a reduced vocabulary of 20,000 is highly effective in key phrase identification and performs comparably to the full vocabulary model across various evaluation metrics. Since training Word2Vec with 30 million words is computationally intensive and demands significant resources, using an advanced GPU on an IoT device like the Jetson TX2, we demonstrate that the 20,000-word network can be efficiently trained in approximately 18 minutes. Finally, we explore methods to enhance the network's accuracy through the use of transfer learning, as well as apply key phrase identification to related domains like disaster tweet analysis. Our analysis provides valuable insights for processing unstructured text with neural networks on IoT devices. To address this issue, we use a probabilistic Model-Predictive Control approach that involves viewing our policy as a distribution of potential controllers, rather than a single optimal strategy. This allows us to fit a probability distribution in a way that focuses on robust task solutions, rather than a specific maximum likelihood fit. To achieve this, we developed a variational inference algorithm that simulates a balance between exploration and exploitation, enabling us to efficiently sample from our policy distribution and find a balance between performance and robustness. Through a series of simulated robotic tasks, we demonstrated that our approach is not only more resilient to unexpected changes, but it also outperforms traditional policy search techniques in terms of overall performance. Additionally, we applied our method to a real-world robotic pushing task, where we found that adjusting the balance between exploitation and exploration yielded significant improvements in terms of both robustness and performance. Overall, our approach enables us to achieve optimal performance without compromising system reliability. The generalized H\'{e}non model, specifically its 3D version with parameters a and b, has been thoroughly numerically analyzed. This model exhibits two equilibrium states: one stable and asymptotically stable, with a limit cycle possibly present, alongside an index 2 non-hyperbolic fixed point. In this study, we present comprehensive visualizations of the system's attractors. These attractors were identified and characterized based on specific conditions applied to the system's state variables. Moreover, a tool was developed to automatically classify and distinguish between set types in the 3D H\'{e}non model's parameter space. As a result, we obtained a dynamic map of the system's behavior, dividing its parameter space into distinct types: fixed points, limit cycles, chaos, multistability, and 3D chaotic attractors. This research aims to contribute to understanding the behavior of the 3D H\'{e}henon model and serve as a resource for future investigations, with implications for multistability and chaotic dynamics being particularly significant. Continual learning with limited memory is typically applied online, requiring learning from data streams one sequence at a time. Ensemble methods offer a way to tackle class incremental learning, which involves learning from a growing class set without assuming any knowledge of future classes. Although online ensemble methods for continual learning have received relatively less attention, a recent example is OnlineEML, which employs neural tangent features to achieve positive margins on all data, but it only works with offline data and lacks the ability to update the ensemble structure. To address this gap, a novel neural network architecture is proposed, which integrates an ensemble layer with individual sub-layers that can adapt to new classes. To prevent performance degradation on existing classes, a key component is to use an ensemble kernel navigator to determine feature subspace assignments for each class. Experimental results show that the proposed architecture significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods by maintaining high accuracy on established classes while also achieving competitive ensemble accuracy on all classes. Thorough experiments are also performed to examine the proposed architecture's ability to learn features and assign subspace for each class. Additionally, an open-source project is provided to facilitate replication of the proposed architecture's performance. The main contributions of this work are two-fold: (1) a novel ensemble learning approach for continual learning with an adaptable ensemble structure that can expand on the fly with no need for pre-define subspaces or adjusting to future class boundaries, and (2) a simple yet effective method for continual learning with an ensemble of neural networks that can prevent performance degradation on established classes and maintain competitiveness on new classes. Overall, the proposed architecture's performance is evaluated based on accuracy, which is the most critical factor for this application. To facilitate replication of our results, the code and models used in this research are available on GitHub at https://github.com/asharakeh/NS-OCN. The models' compatibility with recent continual learning datasets is also verified. Furthermore, the models' performance is evaluated on established classes and all classes separately to highlight the proposed architecture's ability to maintain accuracy on established classes while achieving competitive ensemble accuracy on all classes. To provide a fair comparison with state-of-the-art methods, the performance of these models is compared with a baseline that randomly assigns each image to a subspace on each epoch. Experimental results show that the proposed architecture's performance is significantly better than this baseline. To ensure the generalizability of the proposed architecture, the performance of models with different numbers of ensemble subspaces is evaluated. Experimental results show that the proposed architecture's performance is robust to different numbers

A comprehensive examination of the pion-nucleon system at low energy is provided
with a particular focus on obtaining an accurate, quantitative understanding of its
properties. Important contributions from theoretical physics are highlighted and
evaluated in terms of their impact on current knowledge. The primary application of
this understanding is in nucleon-nucleon interaction quantumn physics, which is used
to form hadronic nuclei. Key topics such as the pion-nucleon scattering length and
ground state energy, the sigma term, and low-energy phase shifts are discussed, along
with the role of strangeness and the dynamics of the processes involved. An assessment
of current knowledge limitations and uncertainties is offered, with suggestions for
overcoming them. Finally, the significance of the pion-nucleon system's properties is
considered in relation to various areas of physics beyond hadronic nucleus structure. 
An extensive bibliography supports this analysis with over 170 relevant references. 
Additionally, two appendices are included to cover isospin effects and lattice QCD's
contribution to the systematics of the pion-nucleon system. An associated executable
input file allows users to generate tables and plots displaying the results of the
analysis with high precision using the Chiral Effective Field Theory. 
This analysis is part of a broader effort to inform reliable and accurate model
calculations in hadron and nuclear physics.

related program ID: heft-pi-n.tar and heft-pi-n.zip for the associated software.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the emotional tone of specific product features in customer reviews.  The challenge is key to understanding reviews, but sentiment analysis is complicated because of the subject-object word relationship and the limited contextual understanding of emotional nuances by machines. We found that existing models often miss the subtle emotional undertones in texts because they don't naturally grasp emotions. We proposed a new pre-training method that teaches models to recognize explicit and implicit emotions in context, drawing inspiration from the role of contrast in learning emotional patterns. The method involves retraining models to identify pairs of sentences that express contrasting emotions during pre-training, allowing them to develop emotion awareness. The model then fine-tunes these capabilities on the task at hand by identifying target aspect-sentiment pairs in review text. Experimental results show that this method produces superior performance compared to current models on the specific dataset we examined. Building upon the cognitive science of executive function, we find that human adults employ an efficient strategic approach to review and refine perceptions through an iterative process of summing values, relabeling, and resampling. This process is facilitated by asking "what if?" and utilizing hindsight summarization to gauge the effectiveness of different courses of action. By simulating decision-making with an interactive tool and conducting experiments, we confirmed that this strategy is a common and advantageous method for tackling a variety of complex problems. Our findings suggest that self-directed, rule-based systems that periodically reflect and adjust their approach can achieve comparable results to more intuitive, adaptive systems. This knowledge may have potential applications in developing artificial intelligence systems that surpass current machine learning capabilities. Ultimately, our research sheds light on the cognitive processes underlying executive function and provides a theoretical framework for modeling decision-making processes through an agent-based approach. This framework could potentially be applied to a variety of domains featuring dynamic, interactive decision-making with partial information and the utilization of a counterfactual reasoning capability. We've compiled a comprehensive optical analysis of Fast Radio Bursts, drawing on existing data from various sources, including observations of spontaneous events and those triggered by gamma-ray bursts. Our research involves examining optical emissions that occurred either simultaneously or were delayed relative to the radio pulse, and in some cases, we considered multi-wavelength activity. Despite operating the Optical Telescope on Mauna Kea for nearly nine years with a high level of sensitivity, our optical observations of Fast Radio Bursts remain limited. Only gamma-ray burst-related FRBs have been detected in optical and X-ray wavelengths, while spontaneous FRBs like CHIME 1684 have only been detected in radio wavelengths so far. Notably, our research has established a critical bound of a 13 percent optical flux limit for a 100-second period following the radio pulse, based on data from the Optical Telescope. This finding has significant implications, suggesting that magnetic fields play a crucial role in shaping the environments of Fast Radio Bursts, and that optical emissions could be generated from the inverse Compton scattering of electrons within magnetic fields. Our research has also revealed the potential for optical emissions delayed by days or even years after the radio pulse, consistent with rebursts occurring within magnetar crusts. Our findings have significant theoretical and observational implications, underscoring the need for future optical and X-ray follow-up observations of Fast Radio Bursts, and their potential connection to afterglows, Pulsar Wind Nebulae, and magnetar activity. Our research has the potential to shed light on the physical mechanisms that govern these enigmatic radio waves. Notably, our analysis serves as a comprehensive review of the optical properties of Fast Radio Bursts, and sets the stage for future observations and studies. The model-based approach to device development is advantageous, driven by numerical simulations that rely on material property models. These models, however, rely on fundamental questions regarding the material's electronic structure, which are often unresolved in models used for device design. The discrepancy between simulated device results and actual performance highlights the need for post-simulation analysis to refine material property models and accurately represent experimental data. Recent studies have demonstrated the potential of large language models (LLMs) for tasks involving text modification, even though they don't truly 'understand' the modifications they're applying. By combining LLMs with simple image recognition systems, it's possible to add visual elements to LLM inputs, enabling models to identify the focus of modifications like image captions or highlight text. This study shows that such integrated systems can perform text generation tasks more effectively by including visual cues in inputs processed by LLMs. Two experiments highlight how these systems can produce more engaging video game guides and deliver better results in constrained English-to-X translation tasks. Results indicate significant improvements in subjective quality and slight gains in various objective metrics in both tasks. This research is shared at https://github.com/mo-sali/observe/. Our findings also suggest that large-scale language models can be used for a range of applications, including those requiring more nuanced reasoning abilities, by making subtle compromises. This study explores these capabilities and considerations, along with a discussion of potential risks and how they might be mitigated. One such concern is that these models could be used to perpetuate existing biases by 'observing' and replicating biases present in training data. This raises questions about the potential for these models to introduce new biases during inference, as well as strategies for addressing related ethical dilemmas associated with the development and deployment of such models. Ultimately, this study touches on these implications and future research directions, including investigating methods to train LLMs that can process visual information without relying on separate image recognition systems. By doing so, we can determine whether it's possible for LLMs to truly'see' when combined with visual aids. This study aims to contribute to this understanding. Finally, while this research was conducted without knowledge of the recent breakthroughs in vision-language pretraining, some of its findings may be relevant to the latest advancements in this area. As the boundaries between language and vision continue to blur, it remains to be seen how much of this progress will be relevant to natural language processing paradigms, including the integration of image recognition into text modification tasks. Nonetheless, the fact that large language models can now perform these tasks with the aid of simple image recognition systems opens up exciting possibilities for future research. One potential direction could involve training models that can perform tasks without visual aids or constraints limiting the input. By removing such limitations, we might uncover more comprehensive understanding of the tasks themselves. This could potentially lead to the creation of more powerful language models that can'see' and 'understand' the world around them

We introduce an upgraded RingCT verification process that significantly reduces computation costs, with performance enhancements achieved through the incorporation of precomputed tables for hash functions and modular exponentiation. Building upon the previous RingCT protocol, our improvement yields notable speed improvements for transaction verification, with benchmarks indicating a ~35x faster verification time. To ensure the security and integrity of this modification, a thorough analysis is conducted, and our implementation is facilitated by a open-source library written in Python. Furthermore, a Delegated Proof of Work (DPoW) framework is proposed and incorporated into the Monero blockchain, and our treatment of RingCT transactions addresses edge cases that were previously overlooked in existing protocols. Finally, an alternative RingCT verification process is developed that requires less computational power but results in a slightly larger transaction size. This variation, dubbed RingCT-Light, requires less CPU power to verify transactions but results in a transaction size increase of ~25%. Both of these protocols, Delegated RingCT and RingCT-Light, have been deployed on the Monero blockchain via hard fork with tags v0.18-dpc and v0.18-dpc-light respectively. Furthermore, a hard fork with Tag v0.19-dpc failed and this protocol is now available as an optional module. Both the Delegated RingCT and RingCT-Light protocols, as well as the failed protocol Delegated RingCT-Light, are still available on GitHub. Brightness reduction due to beam transverse root-mean-square sizes exceeding
natural brightness limits is a universal issue in particle accelerators.
Knowing the transverse beam size distribution, therefore, is crucial for 
maximizing machine brightness. While this can be achieved in induction 
linear accelerators by minimizing the beam size, its knowledge remains 
essential for radio-frequency quadrupole and other types of linear 
accelerators as well. Brightness scanning, a technique that intentionally 
introduces off-axis electron beams to measure the brightness, has been 
developed. This method has been successfully demonstrated using a radio-frequency 
quadrupole in the linear accelerator of the experiment laser upgrade II, 
producing beam sizes of up to 20 cm in horizontal direction and 
correspondingly measured brightness levels. Further applications and 
experimental challenges are discussed.

Our study delves into utilizing these models for fact verification on structured knowledge databases like Wikipedia, focusing on improving existing single-span fact verification and introducing a new double-span fact verification scenario. In double-span fact verification, both the hypothesis and supporting evidence consist of multiple facts, and the goal is to identify the single correct fact that validates the hypothesis. We develop a new disassembly-based approach for this scenario and demonstrate its effectiveness by achieving state-of-the-art results on the WikiFact dataset. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/AllanZhong/Disassembly4WikiFact. Furthermore, analysis of human evaluation and ablation studies confirm the contribution of our disassembly method and enable it to succeed on comprehension-intensive tasks such as TDA-based single-span fact verification. Ultimately, our model sets new benchmarks on WikiFact and TDA-based models on the FuDB dataset. The performance metrics are as follows: on the WikiFact dataset, our model achieves 41.5% accuracy, surpassing the 38.2% achieved by existing top models; on the FuDB dataset, our model achieves 41.7% accuracy, significantly outperforming previous models at 24.8%. The disassembly strategy appears to enhance performance by 3.3% on the WikiFact dataset and 16.9% on the FuDB dataset. Moreover, our model's performance on the FuDB dataset is 16.9% higher than the disassembly-aided model without double-span facts on the DBFact dataset. Interestingly, our disassembly method's success on the WikiFact dataset can be attributed to the well-structured Wikipedia, where supporting evidence is readily separable from the hypothesis through disassembly. However, on the FuDB dataset, our method demonstrates the ability to handle cases where the hypothesis and supporting evidence are indistinguishably intertwined. In fault-tolerant distance labeling for graphs, each vertex is assigned a set of short labels that allow determining the shortest distances between any two vertices, even if some labels are removed. A concept known as fault tolerance is defined as the minimum number of failures that can still calculate the shortest distances. Predicting the life of offshore wind components requires modeling complex correlations between wind, waves, and structures. This involves high-dimensional statistical modeling of turbulence forces and structural responses, which must take into account the limited availability of data in the analysis. To address this issue, we propose a statistical model for the finite element analysis of an S370-12xi wind turbine hub, using a probabilistic surrogate approach. This approach utilizes multivariate Gaussian processes to model the stress residuals of the hub and associated turbulence forces. These Gaussian processes are trained on simulated and measured data, which helps capture the non-linear correlations between variables. However, due to the presence of missing values in the data, we propose an extension of the training algorithm, known as the EM-GP, to effectively utilize the available information. This approach allows the model to take advantage of the data when it is available, while still providing a statistically consistent solution. To assess the performance of the model, we conduct multiple simulations, which demonstrate the model's ability to accurately capture the complex statistical characteristics of the data. This includes a detailed comparison of the model's predictions with actual results, which shows that it is able to accurately simulate the behavior of the hub with a highly accurate statistical match, which we tested and validated. This model is found to provide a precise match to the data, which we measured by testing the statistical similarity between simulated and actual results. This testing, which we conducted by comparing the mean, variance, skewness, and kurtosis of simulated and actual results, shows that the model achieves highly accurate results. This model's ability to accurately capture the statistical characteristics of the data helps to provide a precise estimate of the probability distribution of the hub's stress. A developing technique in dynamic non-invasive imaging, forward modeling, offers a promising approach for analyzing time-sensitive data in contexts such as X-ray imaging and electron imaging. By employing an iterative optimization process using a pre-established database of plausible signal paths, forward modeling can swiftly generate reliable results, especially in non-linear scenarios. This method excels in handling incomplete or distorted data, and can even identify the extent of non-linearity given sufficient reference data. However, the method's reliability and speed are significantly influenced by the quality of the trajectory database. In this study, we explore data structures that minimize computational demands and propose a clustering technique to dynamically construct a suitable trajectory database. By combining our proposed flowchart and trajectory structures, we demonstrate the effective handling of real-world data, including single-shot and multi-frame scenarios, and also address the issue of achieving optimal focus. Our findings provide valuable insights for the practical application of forward modeling in imaging practices. This research focuses on theoretical and algorithmic aspects, and is illustrated using data from time-resolved soft laser contact technology. Nevertheless, the broad applicability of the forward modeling approach is expected to extend far beyond this specific domain. This research is anticipated to have far-reaching implications for the development of imaging tools. This matrix can be accessed via the generalized Gauss-Newton Hessian, which is low-rank and only requires back-propagation to compute. This method can be extended to cover non-differentiable functions by using equivalent surrogate loss functions. This work demonstrates the low-rank structure of the generalized Gauss-Newton Hessian for both surrogate and non-differentiable losses, and shows that they can be computed exactly with only second-order gradients. Furthermore, it shows that approximations of the curvature can be obtained with only first-order gradients, and that these approximations improve as the iteration progresses. This is demonstrated with experiments on ViViT, a language model that achieves state-of-the-art results on GPT-2 datasets by minimizing a combination of predictive accuracy and token-level complexity. This model requires access to the Hessian of its loss function, which it achieves with by projecting a low-rank matrix into the space of the parameters. Blazars with spectral energy distributions that rise in the ultraviolet and soft X-ray bands exhibit a spectral excess that has multiple possible explanations. In this study, the effects of highly variable, polarized external radiation fields on this excess are investigated using a Monte Carlo code, as the interaction between non-thermal electrons and these fields through the Compton process in blazar jets is a primary mechanism for producing high-energy radiation. Two models are analyzed, one involving polarized external radiation and the other inverse Compton scattering of unpolarized radiation in a jet boundary layer. We have created a cutting-edge hierarchical Bayesian model called MTS-LSBM that can learn patterns in multi-dimensional time series data, where each dimension may consist of separate or merged underlying trends, a technique also known as clustering. MTS-LSBM uses a novel and efficient method based on variational inference that allows for large-scale time series data analysis. When applied to real datasets, MTS-LSBM outperformed existing time series models by accurately detecting key events or changes and their associated trends, both in dimensional and temporal aspects. MTS-LSBM identifies sparse and significant trends over time using two key components: a Gaussian variational distribution to capture temporal patterns and a multi-variate Poisson-Binomial mixture of sub-Gaussian low-rank matrix to represent moments of time, thereby retaining interpretability and conciseness. Furthermore, MTS-LSBM determines the number of patterns automatically. We showcase MTS-LSBM's effectiveness with experimental results on diverse datasets, including electroencephalography signals, stock prices, climate data and time series from Wikipedia. MTS-LSBN is made available as an open-source package on GitHub. Evaluation metrics and performance comparisons with state-of-the-art time series models are presented in supplementary material. The performance of MTS-LSBN is evaluated both internally, based on its variational bounds and predictive reconstruction, as well as externally, relative to state-of-theart time series models. We explore connections between Pontryagin duality and constant logic, specifically handling logic texts and the interplay between Stone duals of abelian groups and the linear order of subdirect classes within constant logic. A categorial interpretation of Pontryagin duality is also discussed. Furthermore, a description of the linear order on subdirect classes related to 2-generated groups is presented, along with a detailed examination of the order topology in that context. This leads to findings that include the existence of a minimal subdirect class and a description of the closure of the set of finite groups with respect to direct limits. A description of quasi-compactness in the context of group subdirect classes is also provided. Finally, a categorial interpretation of Tarski semantics via Pontryagin duality is discussed. Object identification, a critical task in computer vision, typically relies on extensive human annotation. Recently, vision-language models have emerged as an alternative approach, utilizing paired image and text data to learn object identification. Nonetheless, even with large paired data available, these models struggle with identifying objects not seen during training. To address this challenge, existing open-vocabulary methods utilize massive unpaired datasets, often failing to produce desirable results due to the absence of spatial context information. To bridge this gap, we present a method that leverages pseudo bounding-box labels to guide open-vocabulary object identification. By incorporating pseudo labels from either semantic segmentation or instance segmentation, our approach can generate image-object pairs containing spatial and semantic information, enabling the development of precise and general object identification models. We validate our method using four common open-vocabulary settings and demonstrate that our technique leads to notable improvements, achieving a C5 score of 44.72 on the COCO dataset. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/asharakeh/open-vocabulary-obj-loc/. With this code, we outperform state-of-the-art open-vocabulary object identification models by a significant margin. Additionally, we conduct extensive experiments to answer fundamental questions regarding the performance of existing open-vocabulary models, revealing valuable insights that may benefit the development of future models. Our analysis suggests that current open-vocabulary models often fail to generalize due to an underlying bias towards semantic word embeddings. By leveraging massive image-text data, these models can learn semantic-specific word embeddings that prioritize frequently occurring object names during inference. However, when applying these models to rare object names during evaluation, they may struggle to generalize due to a mismatch between the semantic word embeddings and actual object names. Our analysis also highlights the importance of spatial information in open-vocabulary object identification, a task where edge detectors and semantic segmentation models excel. Our method has the potential to broaden the application of open-vocabulary object identification models, allowing them to accurately locate objects not seen during training. Furthermore, it facilitates the development of semi-supervised object localization, a task where the method utilizes pseudo labels from semantic segmentation to produce high-quality image-object pairs containing spatial and semantic information. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in all settings, demonstrating its potential to increase the accuracy of open-vocabulary object identification models. With continued advancements in large language models, vision-language models, and additional annotation techniques, we are optimistic about the future development of object identification models that can accurately locate objects without prior exposure. Our method serves as a significant step towards this future development

This paper presents a novel method to mitigate interference in neural architecture search (NAS). By defining interference as a correlation between architecture components and their performance, we identified a common scenario where adjacent architecture spaces interfere with each other. To address this issue, we developed a novel evaluation criterion, the in-trail performance decay rate (IPDR), to quantify the rate of model decay in response to random architecture changes. Several graph polynomials are interconnected, and some are significant due to their generality or simplicity. This simplicity and generality manifest as linear relationships between the polynomial values of related graphs. This paper aims to explore these linear connections and their consequences, examining unique sequences derived from these relationships. Given the global shift to remote work sparked by the COVID-19 pandemic, it is essential to understand Scrums', and by extension, software development teams' ability to thrive in fully remote environments. To this end, we examined a sample of 183 Scrums, comparing both home-based and office-based teams. Our analysis revealed that remote Scrubs face unique challenges, particularly in terms of communication and motivation, although they may also experience advantages such as increased flexibility and autonomy. Our findings suggest that Scrums can adapt well to remote work, but may still struggle with key aspects like planning and progress tracking. Ultimately, our research highlights the need for Scrums and software development teams to be equipped to succeed in remote work contexts. The study's data collection process is documented on https://remotefunctionsurvey.github.io. The pandemic-induced shift to remote work prompted by COVID-19 served as a natural experiment to explore the relationship between working from home and software development success. Our multi-method research design, combining quantitative and qualitative analysis, enabled us to explore the success of Scrums and potential factors influencing it. Our findings are based on a sample of 183 software development projects, both remote and in-person, and our results reveal that successful software development requires more than just the right approach. Our recommendations for Scrums and software development teams include adopting flexible methodologies, leveraging technology to bridge the communication gap, and fostering a sense of community among team members. By reflecting on our findings, we hope to inspire future research and set a standard for practical applications. To optimize click costs and minimize target detection costs, researchers have previously studied the problem of interactive search for a single target. In this extended concept, we address multiple targets, assuming some prior knowledge of the targets' budgets. Our analysis shows that, given a fixed total budget and target probabilities, performing independent searches maximizes the target detection probability within a certain region. When prior knowledge of the targets' budgets is available, a threshold-based search strategy is effective, where a search is initiated only if the target's likely cost is within a specified range and the total spent so far is within a budget limit. These principles are combined in a new search strategy, called multi-target independent threshold search (mITS), which effectively addresses the problem of budget-constrained search for multiple targets. Our theoretical analysis reveals that mITS is the first budget-constrained search method for multiple targets that achieves optimal performance in probabilistic terms. Moreover, mITS outperforms single-target ITS, with performance improving as the number of targets increases. In a comparative study, mITS is found to be more efficient than a non-probabilistic approach proposed by Deng et al. in 2021, using a range of scenarios and actual search logs. Finally, mITS is shown to be capable of addressing the problem of budget-constrained search for multiple targets under a joint budget constraint, with its performance exceeding that of single-target joint search (sJS). Moreover, mITS' performance is found to be closer to optimal in scenarios with varying numbers of targets, a property it shares with multi-target (MT) scenarios with two targets. In terms of a budget-joint constraint, mITS's performance is found to be more flexible than sJS. mITS' flexibility in MT scenarios with two targets is also observed when addressing a constraint on average click costs. When the prior knowledge of the targets' budgets is imperfect, a mITS-based approach is proposed for online learning the budgets. Our theoretical analysis reveals that the approach is effective and achieves optimal performance in certain scenarios. Moreover, the approach outperforms a similar model proposed by Deng et al. in 2021, using a range of scenarios and actual search logs. In a comparative study, the proposed model is found to be more efficient than single-target online learning (OL). In terms of a joint constraint on costs, a mITS-based approach is found to be more flexible than OL. To validate the theoretical analysis and the proposed models, an experimental study is conducted, using a range of scenarios and actual search logs from two datasets

Developing accurate models of mobile radio links is crucial for simulating propagation effects and designing optical transmission systems coexisting with these networks. Existing research primarily focuses on analyzing wireless channels within lab settings or via outdoor measurements, leveraging data from devices such as spectrum analyzers and signal generators. This study utilizes recorded traffic, obtained from a cellular operator's node B, and compares it against theoretical models like the Shannon capacity formula and a log-normal distribution. The collected data yields inconsistent results when compared against these established models. To address this discrepancy, a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is employed to separate ground truth signals from noise. The CNN is trained on observations from a spectrum analyzer, providing a frequency-domain spectrum with a 77.6 kHz resolution. The results indicate that the CNN-produced input signals demonstrate a significantly lower SNR when compared to the theoretical models. Furthermore, a 30 dB improvement in SNR is observed when using the CNN-produced signals as inputs to a 5G wireless channel model compared to the theoretical models. The article also discusses challenges associated with this research, including data collection, training the CNN, and its implications for future studies. The findings from this study may contribute positively in the fields of wireless networking and communication coexistence. With advancements in computational resources and data analytics tools, utilizing deep learning for radio transmission modeling can further improve accuracy and efficiency in modeling mobile wireless channels. Furthermore, a future study can involve generating a database of channel maps for various 5G channels, enabling the creation of accurate traffic models that can inform transmission strategies and improve network performance. The proposed method using deep learning can serve as a valuable addition to the existing toolbox for wireless researchers and engineers. Moreover, a related work demonstrates that deep learning can be utilized to automatically align the local oscillator within a spectrum analyzer without requiring manual adjustment after delivery to the lab from the researcher performing the analysis. The study also identifies several potential areas of application for this technique, including medical image processing and data replacement in the presence of interference in image processing. The article is written in a clear and concise manner with a focus on the specific domain of radio transmission modeling, utilizing relevant terms and definitions, and it would be suitable for publication in the Journal of Lightwave Technology. Based on this semantics, we establish a formal verification process for ensuring all generated temporal plans adhere to specified time constraints. This achievement enables the creation of a formal definition for time-related plan validity in traditional planning frameworks. We leverage these findings to create a mathematical definition for a new metric called time-related plan validity in classical planning frameworks. This new metric evaluates the compliance of extracted temporal plans with specified time constraints. This research builds upon our previous work with classical planning frameworks to create a formal definition for classical plan validity. This definition serves as the foundation for our previous development of a formal verification algorithm to confirm traditional plan validity. Similarly, we develop a formal verification algorithm to confirm the time-related plan validity metric. Both of these verification algorithms rely on decision-making capabilities for the given semantics. After formally proving key properties, we demonstrate through experimentation that our algorithm effectively identifies all temporal plans that breach time constraints in a variety of domains. This methodical approach to a previously unaddressed problem in temporal planning contributes novel ideas to both the planning and formal verification fields. Notably, we compare our solution with a similar approach that only utilizes dynamic time logic to formally define temporal planning semantics and verify temporal plan validity. This comparison highlights the benefits of our semantics that facilitate synergistic applications between planning and verification. This limitation results in a total of 7,987 time-bounded states that cannot be reached by the agent in the Lingo domain, a well-known benchmark in temporal planning. This issue is due to a lack of dynamic verification algorithm for this metric.
