In recent years, SPARQL machine translation has gained significant attention, but translating complex queries remains a significant challenge. Most existing approaches focus solely on the query or use fixed, manually-defined knowledge bases. We introduce an innovative model called SPARQL-DS, which incorporates a dual copying system to adapt to both queries and knowledge bases. This allows the model to learn and update the parts of the knowledge base relevant to each translation task. We also introduce various copying system configurations to facilitate SPARQL translation. We evaluated SPARQL-DS on two datasets - QuAD and QALD - and compared its performance with existing state-of-the-art approaches. Experimental results indicate that SPARQL-DS achieves competitive or superior performance across all metrics considered. Notably, it surpasses state-of-the-art methods on both query and knowledge base adaptation metrics in one of the datasets. We also introduce an adaptable knowledge base extension configuration, which allows SPARQL-DS to achieve zero-shot adaptation on the QuAD dataset that involves multiple knowledge bases. We observed significant improvements in both query and knowledge base adaptation metrics. Furthermore, we performed an in-depth error analysis of SPARQL-DS to shed light on its performance. We observed that the model's performance is largely influenced by the type of token involved in the query, with better performance observed for complex and resource tokens, and lower performance for predicate tokens. We attribute this to the inherent complexity in translating SPARQL queries with multiple variables and constraints. We also observed that the model's performance is sensitive to the size of the knowledge base, with better performance on tasks involving a large knowledge base. We believe that the proposed SPARQL-DS approach offers a promising foundation for translating SPARQL queries with varying levels of complexity. The objective of tensor completion is to reconstruct missing data from incomplete tensors, a problem that arises in various fields, including optics and neurophysics. Typically, tensors are designed to capture 2-D data patterns, like image features, which are often organized in a matrix structure (the 2nd order tensor) to facilitate pattern detection and matching. However, data from cameras, eye movements, or streaming inputs can present as 1-D data sequences requiring transformation into a tensor format. This presentation introduces a novel, streaming method for completing 1-D data sequences by converting them into 3-D tensors, which are then completed by leveraging a self-improving mechanism that tracks patterns. This approach enhances the state-of-the-art by increasing completion accuracy and executing faster, while also relying on fewer parameters compared to existing methods. Moreover, our technique benefits from scalability, which is advantageous for applications involving large datasets. Experimental findings demonstrate that our technique surpasses state-of-the-art methods, which is also supported by theoretical justifications. These concepts have the potential to contribute to further advancements in tensor completion and related areas. Implementation details and the code are available online. Analysis and experimental findings reveal that our technique is particularly effective in cases with missing center data and limited pattern extensions. Additionally, our findings indicate that reliance on a few initial patterns is not necessary, which is beneficial for applications involving limited data sets. We examine a novel problem referred to as the Iterative Graph Normalization Problem (IGNP). Given a weighted graph and a parameter $d$, IGNP involves identifying the largest subset of vertices whose removal results in a subgraph where the degree of each vertex does not exceed $d$. This problem is an extension of the Maximum Weight Independent Set problem and has applications in filtering data and graph-based data visualization. In this study, we propose an efficient algorithm to solve IGNP and provide a comprehensive analysis of its theoretical and practical implications. Experimental results confirm that our method effectively addresses vertices that are outliers or distractions and efficiently handles graphs with diverse structures. Moreover, we discuss the significant influence of IGNP through an exploration of theoretical properties and potential applications in graph-based data visualization. Specifically, we introduce the Iterative Graph Normalization and Visualization (IGNV) approach, which incorporates edge removal as an additional vertex normalization criterion. Consequently, IGNV effectively normalizes a graph to facilitate efficient and scalable visualization. Thorough experimental evaluations using synthetic and real-world datasets highlight the effectiveness of our methods and provide practical recommendations for their use. The proposed algorithms have been successfully implemented and made available online through the Java-based Graph Tool (GT) package. The graphical user interface of this tool enables users to interactively apply our methods to graphs for visualization and data analysis purposes. Furthermore, we provide accessible URLs to enable online exploration of our methods in action, specifically demonstrating their applicability to social network analysis and gene regulatory network visualization. In addition, we provide a concise description of our methods and data analysis examples in PDF form for distribution and sharing. The presented work not only contributes to theoretical and practical advancements but also facilitates the translation of graph structure and vertex attribute-based models into applicable graph analysis and data visualization approaches. Ultimately, the experimental results in this study provide valuable insights and enable the evaluation and generalization of our graph analysis and data visualization methods to novel scenarios. The primary contribution of this study lies in the translation of graph analysis and data visualization concepts to practical applications, and the study's success inspires the exploration of additional graph analysis and visualization challenges. Our capacity to interpret images is unaffected by severe transformations like
reflection, rotation, and zooms as long as the image's essence remains intact. 
Despite this, most current AI models struggle to adapt to such severe 
transformations, especially when identifying objects within images. 
Unlike humans, these models have no built-in capacity for invariance learning 
against severe transformations. Existing AI models can mimic this capability 
only by generating numerous synthetic images during training, a process known 
as data augmentation. To develop AI models that can automatically learn about 
severe transformations, we investigate whether data augmentation is sufficient 
or if there are other techniques at play. By employing behavioral analysis, we 
discovered that both humans and AI models respond differently to severe 
transformations. Furthermore, we found that both humans and AI models can learn 
about these transformations both from the images themselves and from the 
corresponding labels. Our results show that both factors contribute to the models 
ability to identify objects within images. Our findings have implications for 
both the training of AI models and understanding how our brains process images. 
All our code is available at https://github.com/amberla/severe-transforms.

Systems capable of interpreting the meaning of language can operate in two distinct modes - task-oriented and meaning-oriented.  Task-based interpreters prioritize achieving a desired outcome, such as answering a question, and are commonly used in applications where there is access to labeled data.  However, they struggle to perform when applied outside their trained scope.  In contrast, meaning-based interpreters prioritize capturing language meaning, and have the advantage of being able to generalize better, even in cases where there is limited labeled data.  Unfortunately, training systems of the latter type can be challenging due to the lack of suitable datasets.  To address this limitation, researchers have developed Partial-PC, a technique for training interpreters that relies on minimal supervision.  By pre-training the interpreter on incomplete information and using partial supervision, Partial-PC is able to learn the underlying language structure and meaning, and requires only balanced labels for fine-tuning.  Experiments conducted using Amazon Product Reviews and Wikipedia categories data demonstrate that Partial-PC achieves better results compared to existing methods.  Moreover, results indicate that even when only class labels are available, Partial-PC can still be used effectively to train a semantic interpreter.  Additionally, this method allows for natural-sounding, meaning-oriented responses to be generated in a task setting where it would normally require significant supervision to achieve.  Notably, Partial-PC achieves better performance with only 20% of the supervision required by PC, and is able to maintain a comparable gap with much less labeled data.  Observations suggest that Partial-PC is able to capitalize on structural similarities between different tasks.  Further analysis reveals that Partial-PC is able to fill in missing information based on the partial supervision provided during pre-training, and can achieve this without requiring full pre-training.  In experiments conducted using the WebChild dataset, results indicate that Partial-PC can achieve good performance even after only one set of pre-training iterations.  Ultimately, this method allows for more natural, less verbose responses to be generated in a variety of settings, and has the advantage of being able to generalize well even in cases where there is limited labeled data available.  Non-balanced supervision is required for pre-training, and partial supervision is sufficient for fine-tuning.  Further details on the datasets and models used in these experiments can be found online at public repositories maintained by the research authors.  Interestingly, results suggest that systems of the type PC, even when trained on a large dataset, are still unable to generate natural-sounding, meaning-oriented responses in task settings.

This study delves into the workings of a novel decentralized trading platform based on blockchain technology, drawing comparisons to continuum exchange theory. We show that a platform's transaction volume is fundamentally determined by a function of the square of the square root of the number of platform users. Moreover, as the platform's user base grows, its transaction volume shares the same proportional relationship with the square root of the total transaction value as a traditional continuum exchange. To validate this user-volume-square relationship, we provide both analytical and empirical evidence. We start by assuming a specific distribution of lot sizes and use game-theoretic methods to maximize the platform's revenue from transactions. Subsequently, we replicate our analytical findings with empirical data from a decentralized trading platform called Binance DEX. Additionally, we offer an alternative empirical approach that relies on machine learning algorithms for analysis, utilizing data from Ethereuem and Bitcoin networks. Our analysis yields the user-volume-square relationship as a robust and consistent conclusion across both methods. We also offer a novel comparison of blockchain and traditional exchanges, highlighting distinct differences in their transaction volume growth patterns. Our study contributes to the existing body of knowledge on blockchain technology and decentralized trading platforms by offering a quantitative empirical analysis of their performance. It sheds light on the scalability limitations of decentralized systems as platforms grow, underscoring the need for further research on the subject. Moreover, our analysis provides a framework for comparison of blockchain and traditional exchanges, enabling a deeper understanding of their respective market dynamics. Ultimately, our study serves as a starting point for future research on the subject, encouraging readers to explore and develop new insights. We believe that our analytical and empirical findings have significant value in understanding the market dynamics of decentralized trading platforms, while highlighting the need for further empirical investigation to deepen our knowledge of blockchain-based systems. A new metric, the E-value, has been created for analyzing missing data under various Bayesian models. This metric effectively captures the impact of missing data assumptions on Bayesian inference. Here, we develop and evaluate this metric within the context of Bayesian missing data analysis. The E-value is first adapted for Bayesian model-comparison purposes in the context of missing data. The second part of our analysis involves generating synthetic data to assess how well the E-value reflects actual error rates in classification scenarios with missing data. The results indicate that the E-value provides a reliable estimate of error rates in such situations. The efficacy of the E-value is also demonstrated through its application in a real-world example involving the identification of genetic risk factors for schizophrenia, highlighting its practical value in handling missing data assumptions under Bayesian frameworks. The findings suggest that the E-value can be a valuable tool for Bayesian inference in statistical modeling, especially in situations where data assumptions become uncertain. The analysis also sheds light on the relationship between information theory and Bayesian inference in the context of missing data. In seismic reflectivity inversion in practice, we often encounter the issue of nonuniform sparsity, where low frequency components are more significant than high frequency ones. However, the existing sparse regularization methods are designed for uniform sparsity only, and applying them to the nonuniform case results in the suppression of desired low frequency information. To tackle this problem, we propose a new network architecture called NuSPAN, which utilizes a Proximal Average Network to approximate the nonuniform sparsity pattern and can be effectively trained from data alone. The results show that NuSPAN outperforms the existing method by 0.38 in normalized root mean square error (NRMS) and 0.27 in cross correlation (CC) on the Marmousel 2D dataset, and its frequency response is more natural and comparable to human perception. Additionally, NuSPAN is applied to seismic deconvolution and waveform inversion with impressive outcomes. The source code is available online at the specified repository.

This study develops a new principle, the hidden inverses protocol, to rectify errors in multi-qubit operations and demonstrates its application in superconducting quantum devices. When a faulty gate is initiated with a specific initial state, its corresponding inverse gate automatically emerges with a distinct opposite state, unmasking the error and allowing for easy correction. This discovery, initially proposed for ion trap systems, is now adapted and showcased in superconducting quantum devices. Furthermore, experiments and calculations have been performed to validate the effectiveness of the protocol in various quantum circuits, including those used for single-qubit operations, bell state creation, and controlled operations. Notably, even in cases where there's no specific initial state for uncovering errors, partial information about the faulty gate can still be obtained. This research also investigates how the precision of gate inverses changes with distinct initial states and finds that the protocol's robustness can be enhanced by utilizing the right set of initial states, which is then related to the protocol's cross-talk tolerance. This protocol offers a promising solution for detecting and correcting errors in various quantum circuits, especially during the preparation of entangling gates. Moreover, numerical simulations indicate that the protocol's advantages can be realized with current superconducting quantum devices, similar to those used in experiments with fewer than ten qubits. Additionally, we also identify a few instances where the universal applicability of this property to total equivalence relations is exception. Ultimately, we also establish a distinct dual correspondence between the forms of minimal elements within these total relations and the forms of maximal elements in the case of the dual context. We have developed a new ImageNet dataset, which we call DIREC-1, that is comprised of 100,000 images with specified direction. Our research involves introducing the first end-to-end deep neural network that leverages directional information, known as the Directional Convolutional Network (DCN). The DCN is designed to be rotationally invariant by locally adjusting convolutional filters to capture patterns recurring in different directions. Evaluations on the DIREC-1 dataset demonstrate that the DCN outperforms traditional rotational invariant methods. Additionally, we establish a new dataset called DIVision, which is an extension of the DIREC-1 dataset without augmentation. Our results show that the DCN outperforms state-of-the-art models. Moreover, we utilize the DCN as a feature extractor to develop a new rotational invariant model, which we call the RIFEX. Our experiments reveal that the RIFEX outperforms state-of-the-art models on standard ImageNet datasets. All code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/DeepHoG/DirectionConvolutionalNetworks. Our previous research significantly sped up Sinkhorn iteration by taking advantage of a kernel matrix's inherent properties, transforming its $O(N^2)$ complexity to $O(N)$ efficiency. This paper delves deeper into kernel matrix characteristics by defining and applying two key concepts, Lower-ColLinear and Upper-ColLinear, which can respectively identify and create triangular matrices with lower or upper diagonal elements varying linearly, and the operation of multiplying such a matrix by a vector as being either left or right proportional. These definitions enable us to precisely calculate optimal transport using the Nyström method, resulting in computations that are both efficient and accurate to a great degree, specifically to a $O(1/N^2)$ accuracy for large $N$. Recent years have witnessed significant growth in the research of entropic discontinuities of systems of conservation laws and their application to deflagration and detonation shock waves. Although a few contractive conditions have been proposed, they have been found to be either too narrow or too burdensome for use in the standard construction of vanishing momenta. In this paper, a new approach is taken to develop contractive conditions for general conservation law systems, as well as specific standard constructions for the Broadwell model and the five-equation compressible Euler equations. Furthermore, through a novel interpretation of L1 and L2 norms in the definition of entropic discontinuities, it is demonstrated that small initial data will result in vanishing momenta under both new and existing standard constructions. In particular, it is shown for the first time that the L1 norm may be employed to define entropic discontinuities without requiring the strict continuity of entropic functions. Lastly, numerical simulations are performed to verify the results for the Broadwell model and the Euler equations. We hope that these findings will contribute to a deeper understanding of entropic discontinuities, as well as provide insights into designing numerical schemes for issues like detonation and rarefaction waves. We also address a theoretical limitation of existing work, attributing it to a requirement for numerically consistent and potentially contractive schemes to be free of "stiffness". Such a condition was previously assumed necessary for the standard construction approach. We have successfully demonstrated the feasibility of entropic discontinuities defined by small data using both new and existing contractive conditions, potentially paving the way for a relaxation of this theoretical limitation. Nonetheless, further research is needed to fully address this issue. In the case of the Broadwell model, it is found that the L1 norm leads to a contractive condition that is similar to the "stiffness" notion, suggesting that the generation of vanishing momenta via standard constructions may be possible even when such "stiffness" is present. We reserve judgment on this matter for future work. Numerical simulations suggest that while the L1 norm results in a contractive condition for small data, it may lead to less accurate solutions compared to the L2 norm, which is typically employed in previous studies. We hope that the results presented here will contribute to a deeper understanding of entropic discontinuities and their application to issues like detonation and rarefaction waves. We also aim to further investigate the "stiffness" condition and its implications for entropic discontinuities in future work

We explore novel view generation -- a fundamental problem in computer vision -- using a single image perspective. Current approaches that utilize multiple views and non-data driven techniques are either restricted by their reliance on additional images or plagued by inaccuracies and a lack of global consistency. To address these limitations, we have developed DiffDreamer -- a conditional diffusion model that leverages a single image perspective to generate novel viewpoints. By leveraging the robustness of diffusion models, we have tailored DiffDreamer to 1) develop highly realistic and semantically sound 3D shapes and 2) generate novel viewpoints that are synthetically and topologically correct. To facilitate model development, we have created Syn3D -- a comprehensive, human-annotated dataset that pairs synthetic images with complex view angle transformations. Through a series of experiments conducted on Syn3D and other benchmark datasets, we have demonstrated DiffDreamer's superiority over existing novel view generation methods in multiple aspects. To facilitate future research, we have publicly released Syn3D -- a valuable resource that is not currently available. It can be accessed at https://diffdreamer.net. The code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/quantimia/diffdreamer. The repository contains supplementary material, including 3D model animations. To ensure reproducibility, we have made all relevant configuration files available. The work presented here has been developed into a commercial product called Dreamview by Quantimia. With Dreamview, we have powered several high-profile collaborations with top advertising agencies, enabling their clients to generate realistic novel viewpoints for products in virtual 3D environments. To date, our work has been used in the successful development of over 50 commercial projects and trials. Ultimately, we plan to release DiffDreamer's source code under a suitable open-source license, allowing it to be widely adopted in both commercial and academic settings. Until then, we have made available a series of pre-trained, novel view generation models -- each developed using DiffDreamer on Syn3D. These pre-trained models can be used for novel view generation tasks not involving any fine-tuning. To ensure that DiffDreamer outperforms existing novel view generation models, we have made available a set of baseline models -- each developed using DiffDreamer on Syn3D but without any additional training data. To facilitate model selection, we have provided a set of labels -- each corresponding to a specific novel view generation model. These labels can be used for set membership prediction, enabling users to identify the most suitable model for a given novel view generation

Traditional statistical analysis methods for time-to-event data are insufficient for understanding the complex patterns of health outcomes and disease progression in real-time. A new framework called the Multiple State Examination (MSE) is introduced to analyze multiple time-to-event data in a simultaneous examination of past events, providing a comprehensive multidimensional representation of health trajectories throughout a person's life. This innovative approach is illustrated using data from the Framingham Study on the progression of heart disease in individuals, offering a fresh perspective on the multidimensional aspects of cardiovascular disease and subsequent heart attacks. The statistical model developed here is the first to provide an accurate representation of the joint probability of multiple steps in a right-censored time-to-event data, based on historical events, current age, and multiple covariates. This model can be estimated using parametric or semi-parametric methods, with options for incorporating correlations between events in a bivariate and multivariate setting. A simulated example demonstrates the superiority of the MSE model over alternative methods in identifying the associations between events, highlighting its ability to identify clusters of risk factors that contribute to future events. The MSE model's practical significance is further demonstrated by cluster analysis of MSE probabilities, which identifies distinct life-style patterns in the study population. Finally, the MSE model is used to develop practical tools for clinicians and patients, such as personalized risk assessment and classification systems, and tailored prevention and treatment strategies to analyze the joint effect of multiple steps in a person's life trajectory, leading to a heart attack. These risk assessment and classification systems are shown to be more effective than existing methods in identifying the associations between past events and future risks, while offering a valuable tool for clinicians to develop individualized prevention and treatment plans. Using the MSE model, researchers identified seven distinct clusters of risk factors that contribute to a heart attack, including a cluster of highly correlated risk factors such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and high blood sugar. The MSE model's ability to analyze the joint effect of these risk factors was found to be more effective than analyzing each factor individually in identifying the associations between past events and future risks. The application of deep neural networks in medical image classification has shown significant promise due to their advanced image processing capabilities. However, current deep learning methods have limitations when dealing with noisy labels, which can lead to compromised model performance. To address this issue, we propose an approach that utilizes Bayesian statistics to detect and correct noisy labels, thereby maintaining high accuracy even in the presence of label noise. Our method is particularly suitable for medical image datasets, as it involves manually reevaluating the predicted outcomes based on the posterior probability distributions for each class. We implement this approach in a modified LeNet-based model and evaluate its performance using two medical image datasets, achieving impressive accuracy well beyond the robust-OR threshold in both cases. Additionally, we compare our method with state-of-the-art alternatives and demonstrate its effectiveness through both numerical simulations and experiments using real datasets. To facilitate reproducibility, we provide detailed source code and dataset descriptions to support further research. We also conduct a complementary study that compares our approach with other noise-robust learning methods across multiple datasets, which is documented in a related work titled "Comparative Study on Noise-Robust Deep Neural Networks: An Empirical Analysis". In computing science, a widely adopted technique for breaking down complex problems into manageable parts is the use of recursive definitions.  Often, state-based recursive definitions are subject to constraints regarding the state's progression over time - for instance, a resource may only be accessed a maximum of n times.  Existing logic frameworks fall short in accommodating this requirement, as they typically necessitate explicit verification of timing-related constraints.  In response, a new logic approach is proposed, allowing for the unambiguous specification of recursive definitions along with their temporal boundaries.  This methodology is put to the test in developing a formalized version of PTIME, encompassing both decidability and recursive definitions verification.  The application of this method to a real-world compiler algorithm also highlights its practicality and relevance.  Through a comparison with existing logic languages, it is evident that this approach offers improved expressiveness and a clearer structure.  In particular, a comprehensive set of PTIME axioms is formulated, differing from those of existing PTIME logic only through the incorporation of a non-validity axiom.  As a result, a computationally efficient method is achieved, where a maximum of n interprocedural calls is enforced - equivalent to a complexity of PSPACE.  This efficient method is put to the test in verifying the PTIME completeness of a particular algorithm.  Finally, a prototype implementation is provided, serving as a foundation for developing PTIME optimizers with a formal, verifiable guarantee of correctness.  This prototype's correctness is validated through an independent review, separate from the developer, and the presence of extensive, formally defined documentation.  In particular, a real-world compiler project is used to benchmark the prototype's usability and effectiveness.  In conclusion, a novel approach to state-based recursive definitions with time constraints is presented, yielding a range of valuable outcomes including a formal PTIME theory, a type system, a logic for checking termination, and a tool for verifying algorithm efficiency and a compiler with a formally defined and verified correctness proof.  This method's practicality and effectiveness are demonstrated through its application to a real-world compiler algorithm, resulting in a production-ready compiler with a formally defined and verified proof of correctness.  In particular, a comprehensive collection of formal definitions, including recursive definitions with time constraints, is developed, providing a foundation for future work in algorithm verification and development.  This collection of formal definitions is distinct from existing work in algorithm verification and development due to its explicit incorporation of time constraints in recursive definitions, resulting in a unique and valuable contribution to the field. The behavior of forces acting over long distances in granular matter, specifically in 2D static colonies of disks under Coulomb friction, has been investigated through both theoretical and experimental approaches. By applying the concept of macroscopic electrostatic screening, researchers have found that repulsive forces between particles decrease exponentially with the geometric configuration of the particles, leading to the validation of anomalous screening theory. To confirm these findings, both static and dynamic experiments were conducted on colonies consisting of two and three rows of disks; these results were then compared with theoretical models generated using the method of multiple scattering and a numerical code named \textsc{Gym}nasty. Additionally, equilibrium conditions and repulsive forces were analyzed numerically to explain the geometric dependence of the screening length. Crucially, both experimental and numerical observations conform to the predicted exponential relationship between screening length and colony geometry. Furthermore, an interesting correlation was noted between the screening length and colony size, where the decay rate of a single row colony appears shorter than that of more complex configurations; this observation is also supported by numerical simulations. These investigations into the mechanics of granular matter have resulted in the observation of a previously unreported phenomenon, where long-range interactions are modulated by non-trivial screening lengths that are heavily influenced by geometric structure. Consequently, the potential for applications of this mechanism in the design of self-assembled materials is considerable. Moreover, these findings have paved the way for the exploration of emergent properties in more intricate systems where competition between screening lengths may arise. It is anticipated that these discoveries could potentially contribute to a deeper understanding of these complex systems. To facilitate further investigation, a detailed numerical procedure and associated code, \textsc{Gym}nasty, which was used in conjunction with the contact dynamics method, are made available for research purposes. Furthermore, both experimental and numerical results indicate the presence of force anisotropy due to the geometric arrangement of particles, suggesting the existence of emergent rigidity in these 2D static colonies. Future research directions that could lead to the observation of force isotropy in 3D systems, as well as the exploration of collective modes and screening length correlations, are also discussed. Ultimately, the investigation of collective screening in 2D static colonies has shed new light on the unique mechanics of granular matter, while highlighting potential applications and avenues for further research in the field. In combinatorics, the goal of this research is to establish a relationship between periodic patterns of 2D lattice models and the characteristics of the shapes that emerge from these patterns. We use the example of the 2-component Ising model to illustrate our method, which involves examining the extreme forms of these patterns and using the properties of length distributions to find the necessary information. The COVID-19 pandemic significantly impacted human behavior worldwide.
Understanding how these changes affected urban social dynamics is essential for
characterizing the social consequences of the pandemic. To explore this, we used
unmanned aerial vehicles equipped with autonomous flight capabilities to
collect data on a city center's traffic patterns every two weeks from February to
May 2020, comparing them to a control group from 2019. Our analysis revealed a
decline of nearly 58% in the diversity of species interactions during the
pandemic. Additionally, we found that birds benefited from the altered environmental
conditions, increasing their population diversity. However, this change came at
the expense of other species, which may have been displaced by the changes in
behavior. Further investigation is needed to determine the long-term effects of
these changes on the local ecosystem. To facilitate similar research, we're making
the data available to the public. When social distancing policies were relaxed, the
diversity of species interactions increased, returning to its pre-pandemic level.
This finding highlights the complex relationship between human behavior and urban
ecosystems, which may have been amplified by the pandemic. By using cutting-edge
airborne technology, we've shown that differences in human behavior during the
pandemic can be quantified. Our research has important implications for future
recoveries from crises like the pandemic, which may have lasting effects on
urbanization and human behavior. Ultimately, to maintain complex urban systems,
we must preserve the income diversity of species interactions. A critical factor
in achieving this will be addressing the underlying causes of the changes in
human behavior during the pandemic. To this end, an essential area of study will
be understanding the link between the pandemic and changes in urban social dynamics.

The number of people living in cities is rapidly increasing, with young individuals being more likely to reside in urban areas. Consequently, cities are expanding and becoming more fragmented. Effective management of city growth and fragmentation depend heavily on the design and implementation of urban information systems, which necessitate the integration of multiple perspectives and viewpoints. To address this need, this paper introduces the GUIDES framework, which is a geographic knowledge delivery system designed to support city planning and decision-making through a universal and flexible information architecture. This architecture enables the creation of various geographic information models, which can be utilized in different city-scale applications and approaches while maintaining a unified and consistent framework. GUIDES is implemented using a unique information model based on the concept of layers and viewpoints, which are applied in a city in northern Italy, specifically the Padua metropolitan area. This demonstration highlights the local government's capacity to adapt and respond to city growth and fragmentation by leveraging GUIDES as an innovative city information system, which facilitates seamless, intelligent, and sustainable city development. The emergence of Primordial Black Holes (PBHs) during the early universe could significantly impact current cosmological theories. If PBHs make up a substantial portion of Dark Matter, it could have significant implications for gravitational waves and cosmic structure research. We've developed a computational tool called PopSyCLE that enables efficient calculation of PBH properties and can be used to analyze their potential role in Dark Matter. By incorporating PBHs into Dark Matter models and examining their detectability, we find that in the majority of scenarios, they are not observable through gravitational waves or lensing, but may be detectable through cosmic structure observations and gravitational redshifts. We've obtained a closed-form solution for PBH embedding mass distribution and energy density contribution that is independent of scale factors, allowing for a more accurate understanding of cosmic structure and PBH interactions. Utilizing a Markov Chain Monte Carlo framework, our analysis sets a threshold of $\left(\frac{\sigma_{(2-m_{{\rm PBH})}}}{\sigma_{\psi}}\right)_{\rm mod} \lesssim 0.15\%$ on the variance asymmetry of the matter density field at a $95\%$ confidence level, in agreement with Planck and CMB data. Furthermore, our analysis places a lower bound of $2\times 10^{-11}$ on the PBH mass density fraction based on CMB and galaxy distribution data, providing insights into the PBH Dark Matter hypothesis. We've also demonstrated the PBH mass range in the Dark Matter model to be $[2.4, 3.2]$ and found the mean PBH mass to be $8.9$ in a $95\%$ confidence interval. Additionally, our analysis suggests a lower limit of $5.9\times 10^{-3}$ on the PBH gravitational binding energy fraction and found the gravitational binding energy to be $4.0\times 10^{-4}$. Finally, our analysis indicates that PBHs with a $68\%$ confidence interval of $5.4\times 10^{-5}$ or greater variance asymmetry could potentially be detectable through gravitational binding energy measurements. The developed tools and results provide a foundation for future PBH Dark Matter and gravitational binding energy studies. The code and calculations are available upon request. Recent studies have shown that parameter-efficient models can be highly effective, but adapting models to specific tasks by updating only a few parameters can also lead to subpar performance. To address this issue, we propose a new method called Special Token Adaptation that updates model parameters by introducing task-related tokens and optimizing their embeddings. Our experiments involving transformer models on six datasets in NLP found that STA requires significantly fewer parameters than full model fine-tuning and yields comparable or even better performance in many cases, including improved results on CoQA, SQuAD, TACkit, MS MARCO, T5, TACkit, TACkit, and STS tasks. Furthermore, STA facilitates the creation of "zero-shot" adapters that require no training at all and show a moderate performance drop relative to fully fine-tuned models on some datasets. Our findings indicate that STA has the potential to be a powerful tool for adapting pre-trained language models to NLP tasks in a parameter-efficient manner. The code used in this research has been made available on GitHub. Additionally, our work demonstrates that STA's ability to update model parameters can be extended to other types of pre-trained models such as EL models, and interestingly we found that our approach is not only applicable to NLP tasks but can also be successfully applied to a "low-resource" dataset called the Dataset for the Identification of Similar Textual Meaning Representations. Our research is the first to introduce such a dataset and demonstrates that our approach is highly adaptable, and in some cases, the improved results can be attributed to the removal of biases present in the reference data. Recent studies examining pre-trained language models like BERT and ELMo for part-of-speech tagging and sentiment analysis find they often reject inferior parsing options even without error correction. However, it's unclear how they handle rejection, whether it's an integral part of their language processing or just a fallback. To address this, this study investigates rejection handling in BERT models used for part-of-speech tagging. Through manual evaluation and mathematical analysis of model outputs, it's found that BERT models indeed reject parsing options consistently, with rejection likely resulting from a combination of confidence in option accuracy and compatibility with surrounding context. Interestingly, models tend to prefer one top option over others only when confident in its accuracy. The study also suggests that rejection can serve as a natural language processing mechanism. To facilitate further research, this paper provides a new evaluation metric called RECoP (Rejection Confidence in Parsing), measuring the consistency of rejection under the same input conditions, and finds that this metric correlates with models' task performance, indicating higher rejection confidence is linked to better task performance, with some limitation of this finding. Additionally, this study finds that models tasked with rejection are better at identifying accurate top options and have improved task performance, suggesting that rejection is an integral part of the BERT's language processing capabilities. The study's findings were applied to other models, including BART and ALBERT, with similar results. Key benefits of our approach include its ability to be seamlessly integrated into existing translation systems, adaptable to diverse evaluation metrics, and flexible application to both on-the-fly and post-hoc models. Moreover, our comprehensive evaluations on four prominent datasets, comprising datasets derived from the WMT 2002 Turkish-English and the JRC-ACTIVE dataset collections as well as the official NIST ACTIVE test dataset, showcase the efficacy of our method in improving translation coherence and precision when utilizing various look-ahead distances and evaluation metrics. Additionally, our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art by 2.2 and 1.3 points in terms of coherence and precision, respectively, on the official NIST ACTIVE test dataset. Furthermore, our post-hoc analysis reveals that our method is effective across multiple evaluation metrics, including fluency, coherence, precision, and semantic precision. Key insights from our investigation into the properties of our method involve the impact of the look-ahead distance, the models' ability to consider non-truncated translations, and the exploration of the trade-off between coherence and precision. Hao and Song (2021) proposed the ASP framework, aiming to provide an unconditional exact close form solution to discrete and continuous Asian options under a broad class of Markov changing payment schemes. We initially commend the pioneering work but discover that the pricing formula is actually already a known solution developed by Szegö (1976) and later validated by Shirian and Shao (2015). Moreover, the general nature of the ASP formula relies heavily on a key assumption that the Markov process can be represented as a sum of a polynomial up to the order of n together with an independently evolving sub-process. We note that this requirement may not be met in certain situations, such as when the Markov process is a geometric Brownian motion or a scaled Brownian motion with a deterministic parameter. We then introduce a revised method, referred to as the RAS method, to derive a close form solution to Asian options under a broad class of Markov changing payment schemes. The key features of the RAS approach are the relaxation of the mentioned assumptions and the provision of an unconditionally exact close form solution to a broad class of Markov changing payment schemes including discrete and continuous Asian options. Furthermore, the RAS formula is validated as being free from corrigan numerical singularities, which were present in the original ASP formula. We showcase the effectiveness of the RAS approach by comparing the pricing results and Greeks for fixed and floating average Asian options with those obtained by ASP, semi-closed form solutions and Monte Carlo simulations. Notably, the RAS approach outperforms the other methods in terms of numerical stability and precision. Lastly, we extend the RAS method to derive a close form solution to multi-dimensional Asian options under a broad class of Markov changing payment schemes. Understanding how complex visual models derive meaningful conclusions remains an ongoing challenge. Our work develops upon the notion that examining a network's decision-making processes through transparency and explanation can yield insights into its internal workings and data interpretation. We introduce a novel technique to analyze how a network assigns significance to images when classifying them, and present an innovative approach to identify and isolate the most relevant regions within these images. This method, Latent Visual-Semantic Filter Attention (LVSFA), is built on a versatile attention mechanism that can detect and focus on image details even when the class of interest is not clearly defined. Utilizing this method, we investigate the manner in which networks interpret ambiguous image classes, such as 'dog' versus'sheep', and discover that some networks may focus on the image background. Our study demonstrates that by leveraging explanation methods, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of how models interpret and generalise visual concepts. Experimental results indicate that our proposed concealer delivers the highest available visual quality while maintaining a relatively compact model size. Additionally, we successfully reapply the individual components of our approach to address related problems, demonstrating their versatility and potential for widespread application. Ultimately, we apply our method to the specific challenge of preserving watermark fidelity, with our results showing promising results in multiple configurations. A quasilinear model in the diffusion framework is developed for studying magnetic flux rope formation and solar type II radio bursts in magnetized plasmas. This model unifies electron dynamics with two-temperature ions, assuming both particles and magnetic field follow quasilinear diffusion equations. A conservative finite element method is devised to approximate these nonlinear equations, leveraging the exponential smoothing of energies as a key validation test. This method constructs a fully discrete scheme using the semi-implicit scheme and the Crank-Nicolson time scheme, ensuring conservation of key physical energies. By establishing a fully discrete framework, we prove the existence of a path of fixed points representing stationary solutions, as well as their smooth dependence on parameters. This method is implemented using a time-stepping solver in the PyCLAW framework, augmented with custom electron and magnetic field solvers, and validated via local refinement tests within the Dedalus and PyCLAW ecosystems. This research lays the groundwork for further study of nonlinear magnetized plasma dynamics using the quasilinear diffusion framework and the conservative solver's energetic conservation properties. A future paper will apply this model to simulate solar type II radio bursts and magnetic flux rope formation. A stochastic integro-differential equation is introduced to model a brushing process on a surface. This equation describes the spreading and truncation of an applied substance on a given surface as a result of brushing. When the applied substance reaches a minimum threshold, it no longer spreads and remains on the surface. A numerical solution is developed for this type of equation, which can also be used to approximate a special case of a local semidifferential equation when the applied substance does not truncate. Several illustrative examples are provided to demonstrate the validity and applications of the developed method. Additionally, a comparative analysis of different types of integro-differential processes is conducted based on the obtained numerical results. Finally, an empirical model is developed to describe the spread of lotus leaves on the leaf surfaces of lotus plants. This model is used to simulate the spread of leaves on individual plants and assess the importance of various factors that may influence spread. Moreover, a special case of the empirical model is used to investigate the effects of truncation on spread in a competitive scenario. This model is used to simulate the interaction of two species that compete for space and grow leaves from their roots. This simulation reveals that competitors that do not require space and grow leaves from their roots can outcompete species that require space and grow leaves from their roots or from fixed points. This outcompetition can also lead to a unique pattern of species distribution in which species that do not require space and grow leaves from their roots tend to concentrate towards the roots of the plant. Moreover, a special case of the integro-differential model is used to simulate the spread of a brush in a 3D environment with applications in painting. This simulation reveals that the type of brush used and the direction in which the brush is moved can significantly affect the spread of the brush and the quality of the painting. These factors can be used to create different effects in different paintings. This simulation also shows that species that do not require space and grow leaves from their roots can colonize and infect other species that require space and grow leaves from fixed points. This colonization and infection can also lead to a unique pattern of species distribution in which species that do not require space and grow leaves from their roots tend to concentrate towards the roots of the plant. In various real-world applications such as social media, web links, and phone call records, networks exhibit dynamic behavior with nodes and edges constantly appearing or disappearing over time. This time-varying aspect demands a reconsideration of traditional embedding methods that fail to account for temporal changes. As a result, researchers have proposed evolving graph embedding frameworks that capture both structural and temporal information. This paper aims to provide an exhaustive overview of such methods, which has been lacking in the literature until now. Furthermore, we introduce a unified framework and systematically categorize existing approaches into node, edge, and joint embedding schemes. Additionally, we discuss common metrics used for model evaluation and offer some insights on future research directions. This comprehensive survey is expected to offer valuable insights for scholars working in this area, helping them navigate the vast literature and understand the state-of-the-art in evolving graph embedding. With the rapid growth of network-related challenges and opportunities, this survey is expected to be a valuable resource in the years to come. This state was analyzed as an excitation of the 0+ $^{3}$H ground state, and the first two $^{7}$H excited 0- states were also determined, which have lower neutron binding energies than the $^{3}$H 0+ ground state. The presence of these 0- states in $^{7}$H is a rare occurrence in odd-odd nuclei. Theoretical models, such as the finite range HFB and SHFB, were used to study this phenomenon. The emergence of this structure is attributed to specific single-particle energies required to form the $^{7}$H 0+ ground state and its excited 0- states. The predicted spectra of even-odd nuclei with mass numbers 5-9 support the $^{7}$H structure, suggesting a new perspective on the odd-odd nuclei with mass number 7. Theoretical calculations were used to predict the $^{5}$H, $^{5}$F, $^{6}$He, $^{6}$Be, $^{7}$Li, $^{7}$B, and $^{7}$N unbound states that could exist below the three-nucleon threshold. The predicted unbound states may facilitate the study of three-nucleon continua in mass number 5 and 7 nuclei. The predicted spectra suggest that in the future it will be possible to identify experimental evidence for these unbound states. Machine learning applications often rely on reinforcement learning to mitigate contamination and yield stable outcomes. In cases where contamination occurs, as in medical diagnosis, reinforcement learning can help detect and prevent incorrect data from affecting predictions. This paper explores the issue of contamination on graph-structured data within Graph Neural Networks, focusing on detection rather than prevention for the first time. We demonstrate that a combination of reinforcement learning and graph-based methods is effective in identifying contamination and improving GNN robustness on structured data. This research reveals the possibility of a GNN model achieving 100% accuracy on the structured data dataset, Pinvox, similar to a model without contamination. Additionally, we discovered that a model without contamination but with limited training data still achieves better results compared to a model with a large training dataset and contamination. This breakthrough has significant potential in fields like medicine, where contamination can lead to severe consequences if not properly addressed. We hope this study will inspire further research in contamination-resistant machine learning. In this paper, we address the problem of identifying minimal vertex sets within infinite hypergraphs. A vertex set $S$ is considered minimal for an infinite hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$ if it fulfills two conditions: Firstly, for any hyperedge $H$ in $\mathcal{H}$, $S$ is a subset of $H$, indicating it's a subset of at least one hyperedge. Secondly, for any proper subset $T$ of $S$, $T$ is not a subset of any hyperedge in $\mathcal{H}$, meaning it's impossible to find a hyperedge in $\mathcal{H}$ that contains $T$. We investigate the existence of such minimal vertex sets in all cases and explore their possible structures. Additionally, this study examines the characteristics of hypergraphs with minimal vertex sets in general, including conditions that must be met and those that do not need to be met. We also consider a different type of minimal vertex set where an empty hyperedge is possible and establish its definition and properties along with its relevant applications. Lastly, this research looks at applications of minimal vertex sets in specific contexts. We introduce an inter-domain loss to facilitate semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. Our approach utilizes a CycleGAN to translate speech from one domain to another, enabling inter-domain loss to minimize domain discrepancies. Unlike existing inter-domain losses that introduce additional supervision, our method leverages unpaired speech examples to minimize domain disparities. Experimental results on the SI-ET3E and CSMS-ET5 datasets reveal that our method surpasses baseline performance, with notable improvements on word error rate (WER) - 9% and 6% on SI-ET3E and CSMS-ET5 datasets respectively. Furthermore, our findings indicate that using CyclicGAN-trained unpaired data, speaker-adaptation WER can be reduced by 43% on SI-ET3E. We make our implementation available on https://github.com/theswagteam/CSDGAN-ESR. Our method is also registered on https://arxiv.org/.

For deep active reinforcement learners, choosing when to take actions in the environment is just as crucial as selecting target goals. To tackle this problem, we propose a universal strategy that not only adjusts the exploration-exploitation trade-off but also determines when to curtail learning. To accomplish this, we employed a hierarchical prediction method using neural networks and applied it to the STAR Lunden algorithm in the autonomous navigation of a mobile robot. When testing STAR Lunden with different prediction networks, the results showed that using a unified model across goal selection and action choice leads to better outcomes. Additionally, we found that using a unified model enables goal selection and action choice to benefit from shared learning. Furthermore, we discovered that using a unified model allows for the easy incorporation of additional policies which can aid in emergency situations, such as avoiding obstacles. Overall, our method demonstrated that a single, complex prediction network can effectively manage various aspects of autonomous navigation, paving the way for the creation of more compact and efficient algorithms by replacing multiple components with a single model. Our primary objective is to comprehensively analyze the impact of an error in which a ball is released on viewers' perceptions of a throwing motion. To achieve this, we have developed a novel throwing technique known as "FauxThrow," which allows us to artificially produce authentic-looking throwing motions where the ball's trajectory appears to be inaccurately tracked. By employing FauxThrow and conducting a quantitative experiment through a human-centered approach, we found that specific aspects of overarm throwing motions, such as the point of release, significantly influence observers' estimates of a thrower's skill level and perceived throwing force. Moreover, we discovered that observers' impressions of release location are influenced by factors such as speed, acceleration, and throwing style. These findings could be applied in areas like sports training, virtual reality experiences, and motion capture technology to improve accuracy. Ultimately, the insights gained can contribute to the development of more realistic and interactive virtual human characters. To facilitate the reproduction of our results, we provide an open-source implementation of FauxThrow, along with key algorithmic components, all accessible on GitHub. Our research suggests that modifying the point of release in a throwing motion can give the impression of a thrower applying force from an unconventional part of their arm. Interestingly, we discovered that certain types of throwing styles, such as those characterized by rapid acceleration, are associated with the perception that the ball is released later in the throw. Conversely, slower throws and those characterized by late release tend to give the impression that the ball is released earlier in the throw. These observations have significant implications for the training of virtual agents. To integrate Neural Machine Translation with syntax, a novel parsing method is developed that determines part-of-speech tags, parse trees, and word alignments simultaneously. This new method overcomes limitations of previous approaches by handling uncertain parse trees and multiple word alignments. In experiments with English-to-German translation tasks, it has been demonstrated that incorporating syntax can improve translation performance. Additionally, the method yields high-quality English and German parse trees, exceeding the quality of pre-existing parser models. Further benefits of syntax-based translation are observed in translation tasks involving diverse languages and low-resource datasets. Moreover, the method offers accurate part-of-speech tag predictions that surpass the performance of dedicated tag prediction models. Finally, the method enables automatic detection of word alignments, which confirms existing findings that a significant number of words in the source material do not have corresponding matches in the target material. Further details about the method can be found in the accompanying PhD thesis. All the method's source code and pre-trained models are publicly available on the Open-Source platform GitHub. In particular, the method's decoder is available as the package tdt-sdp. Additionally, the method's parser is available as the package syntactic-tdt-sdp. Several example results can also be found on the website syntaxintranslation.com. In summary, the method yields superior results in translation, parsing, and tag prediction tasks, which are crucial components of natural language processing. It has also been successfully applied to various languages and domains with different levels of syntax complexity. Furthermore, the method's ability to determine part-of-speech tags and word alignments enables the automatic detection of syntax-based translation benefits, which are (1) increased translation accuracy, (2) improved syntax-based translation models, and (3) better data selection through syntax-based translation. Moreover, the method's ability to handle uncertain parse trees and multiple word alignments is an advantage over existing translation models, which often employ greedy decoding to yield a single parse tree and word alignment. In contrast, the method's decoding process involves a combinatorial search that yields multiple uncertain parse trees and word alignments. While this property can lead to slower decoding, it is an essential component of the method's performance. In fact, the method's training objective is designed to overcome this challenge by (1) utilizing stack regularization to reduce the size of the search space, (2) employing a balanced top-down and bottom-up decoding approach, and (3) including a data-driven mechanism to determine when to proceed with stack regularization. In astrophysics, the study of molecular binding energies is crucial for understanding various cosmic phenomena. To facilitate the comparison of experimental and theoretical binding energies, a comprehensive database was developed, exclusively using high-level quantum chemical results. It encompasses the calculations of 119 molecules, encompassing 98 different species, with a total of 574 distinct binding energies, up to the level of double ionization. Each binding energy value in the database is accompanied by an associated error margin and a reference point, enabling the straightforward access to underlying data via related publications. Additionally, a risk-based assessment tool has been introduced to gauge the likelihood of individual binding energy values being available to support future comparative analysis, with a focus on astrophysical applications. Lastly, a comparative analysis of experimental and theoretical binding energies has been conducted, revealing a notable discrepancy between the two methods, with implications for future astrophysical calculations. The database can be found online at https://beap.beckgroup.org/.

The researchers in a recent study derived an expression for the reflection coefficient $R(\xi)$ in terms of physical space variables $u$ and $v$ for the Davey-Stewartson II equations. They were the first to provide a direct link between $R(\xi)$ and the Riemann invariants $r_1$ and $r_2$, yielding the formula $R(\xi)=e^{2\theta_0} \exp(-2K_1(\xi,r_1,r_2))$. Notably, this expression for $R(\xi)$ is valid even when $u$ or $v$ change sign. They also observed that $R(\xi)$ is influenced by the signs of $u$ and $v$, and depends on $|k|$ rather than the direction of $k$, indicating new solutions that arise when $u$ or $v$ becomes negative. Furthermore, by applying new functions $\tilde{\eta}_1$ and $\tilde{\eta}_2$, the authors were able to link the solutions of DSII to those of the SGP equations and discovered a new subclass of soliton solutions that are not present in reference [29]. They were also able to provide a new representation of $R(\xi)$ in terms of $\tilde{\eta}_1$ and $\tilde{\eta}_2$. In addition, the authors were able to generalize the results of reference [27] by showing that the new expression for $R(\xi)$ remains valid even when $u$ or $v$ changes sign. Finally, through numerical simulations, the authors were able to investigate how well these new solutions of DSII match the solutions of the SGP equations, finding that the solutions match perfectly as $|k|$ increases. Our theoretical analysis confirms that these variants possess greater stability than the original network. The efficiency of semantic segmentation in the analysis of rare medical images can be improved through the utilization of augmented images generated by point-intervention techniques. This study explores how these augmentations impact the performance of U-Net-based models in the task of identifying pneumonia within CT scans of the lungs. Preliminary findings indicate that both image-scale and pixel-wise augmentations demonstrate a substantial decline in the required amount of labelled data, while remaining robust against data augmentation. However, pixel-wise augmentations prove to be more effective and suitable for procedures requiring precise boundary information, as they do not compromise the integrity of the original image content. Increasing the application of image-scale augmentations results in superior model performance, yet it may lead to overfitting if not balanced with validation set evaluation. Combining 5x image-scale augmentations with 2x pixel-wise augmentations yields superior performance across all data configurations, making it a versatile and efficient technique for segmentation tasks. This approach enables the creation of highly accurate models using significantly reduced amounts of labelled data, specifically 25 images, thereby facilitating its practical application in the context of rare medical image analysis. This U-Net based method achieves competitive performance, outperforming state-of-the-art models evaluated on the COVID-19 Segmenation Challenge dataset. This technique is proposed to be used in a variety of rare medical image analysis applications, where it may prove beneficial. As AI systems increasingly affect people's lives, it is essential to assess their moral behavior using established concepts of harm. Although the term 'harm' can be interpreted in different ways, we argue that its causal implications should be used to evaluate AI morality since current AI models operate under probabilistic conditions following the axiomatic principles laid out by Allen in 2018. Building upon Allen's work, we define and divide specific types of harm caused by actions with consequences, $H_{ac}$, and actions with effects, $H_e$. Subsequently, we apply various combinations of these definitions to different moral frameworks, such as minimax, utilitarian, and contractualism. By considering both $H_{ac}$ and $H_e$, we demonstrate that these combinations result in distinct moral systems distinct from previous minimax, utilitarian, and contractualist AI morality models. Moreover, we show that using $H_{ac}$ and $H_e$ allows us to distinguish between optimistic and pessimistic variants of utilitarianism, while preserving contractualism unchanged. When incorporating $H_{ac}$ and $H_e$ into different moral frameworks, we identify new moral systems such as Pessimistic Utilitarianism and Contractualism, each with distinct decision-making properties. Our work highlights the significance of a systematic approach to AI morality by adapting established moral definitions to an increasing AI presence in decision-making roles. We believe this to be the first comprehensive study to assess the minimax, utilitarian, and contractualist AI morality models using $H_{ac}$ and $H_e$. We have also developed open-source tools to test and visualize these models for action-based systems to facilitate a comparison with a new model presented in \cite{amor}, which uses $H_{ac}$ and $H_e$ to evaluate effect-based systems. This research presents an investigation of zero-shot voice translation, where spoken language input is directly converted into target languages without pre-identified output languages. Three key challenges - multi-language input, multi-language output, and lack of pre-identified target languages - make voice translation even more complex. To tackle these difficulties, we propose three innovative techniques. Firstly, we devise a new objective function to facilitate zero-shot voice translation across multiple input and output languages. Secondly, we develop a language encoding method via a neural graph. Thirdly, we employ pre-trained acoustic models across multiple languages without necessitating further training. Experimental results on three language pairs indicate that our proposed system is capable of performing high-quality zero-shot voice translation. Furthermore, we have created a new voice translation dataset with 12 languages, termed the Zero-sharp dataset, to facilitate future research. The suppression of elective surgeries during COVID-19 pandemics has led to a significant backlog of patients awaiting orthopedic procedures. However, the routine use of pre-operative images to diagnose and plan operations relies on advanced technologies. To combat the reduced capacity of hospitals, we propose an innovative, efficient method utilizing only image annotations for the tasks of lesion detection and segmentation in COVID-19 affected pre-operative X-ray images. This approach will provide valuable outcomes for patients by identifying potential lesions which could pose a greater risk due to the immune system's weakened state. Given the scarcity of fully annotated data, we suggest a two-stage learning process. First, we use image-level annotations to pinpoint general areas and then refine those predictions using segmentations for final demarcation. By leveraging pairs of fully annotated images and identifying potential lesions from the two previous steps, we can converge the two stages. Experimental results on a COVID-19 dataset confirm the effectiveness of our method and highlight its ability to detect lesions even when they are not explicitly annotated. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial for assessment and simulation in spine conditions. We present a fully automated approach using CT scans to precisely identify vertebrae and calculate their 3D coordinates. By initially extracting candidate vertebral corners through anatomically-constrained optimization, we rectify and align the spine, then apply candidate refinement followed by template matching to identify the correct vertebra. Post-processing involves noise reduction and visualization. This method, with its robust candidate generation and refined refinement, demonstrates high precision and accuracy, achieving 100% identification rate for lumbar vertebrae L1-L5 and 99% for all thoracic and lumbar vertebrae, with an average point-to-point error of 1.45 mm. This performance surpasses current automated methods, with the added benefit of being applicable to both transverse and sagittal reconstructions, expanding its usability to a wider range of imaging data. Additionally, we present quantitative error analysis, showcasing the method's capability to accurately localize and identify vertebrae even in the presence of common spinal imaging variations. This research also provides a foundation for exploring semi-automated adaptations for less common vertebral levels. The proposed method's source code is publicly available on GitHub, accompanied by demonstration videos. However, in situations involving quantum mechanics and radiation, electrons can suddenly change trajectory without changing energy. This phenomenon is known as resonant scattering. In regular conditions, if an electron is brought close to a nucleus with too much kinetic energy, it will repel the nucleus and end up flying off in a different direction without transferring this energy. This means there is no transfer of energy between the electron and the nucleus. When exposed to radiation, however, this rules applies less strictly. This is because radiation has a continuous supply of energy, and this supply can temporarily give the electron extra energy allowing it to interact with the nucleus in ways it couldn't before. In order for this to happen, a precise balance of energies must occur, and this extra energy is temporarily given to the nucleus, in a process known as coherent nuclear resonance rotation. This means there is a small chance that the electron will interact with the nucleus in a way it wouldn't have under regular conditions. We introduce an innovative variational approach to resolve the quantum separability problem using the Hilbert-Schmidt norm, leveraging variational methods. We demonstrate that this method, which employs the Fisher-Rao metric, yields optimal results identical to the HS norm, at significantly reduced computational costs. The majority of calculations can be performed in the classical domain, and the corresponding quantum states can be directly extracted from the optimal solution. Through numerical experiments, we verify that this method surpasses previously suggested HS norm-based max-volume variants. We also observe that one of the most effective protocols, low-rank approximation, is outperformed by incorporating the variational method in high-rank scenarios. These findings are further substantiated by analytical examples illustrating info-max flow, which underpins the method's efficacy in detecting separability in complex systems. Following numerical experiments, we examine the corresponding statistical model in a real-world application, using medical imaging data of eyes to predict diabetic retinopathy. Here again, we find that the variational method outperforms other existing protocols in various system dimensions. Finally, we discuss how the method can be extended to more general norms and higher dimensions, which may offer further improvements. We also explore the corresponding differential geometric framework and provide insights into its potential as a research area, while the associated mathematical framework may contribute to developing novel, innovative protocols in the future. In this research, we explore the issue of overcrowding in home Wi-Fi networks by analyzing the performance of home routers and their connected devices according to IEEE 802.11 standards. By utilizing channel occupation metrics provided by IEEE 802.11k/v, we develop a solution to mitigate congestion. Specifically, our approach involves using the IEEE 802.11k/v measurement tool to identify the optimal access point or extender for each device and automatically adjust settings to minimize congestion. This solution can be easily implemented on existing home Wi-Fi networks without requiring modifications to the network architecture. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed channel load-aware AP/Extender selection method effectively reduces packet loss and improves throughput for both APs and devices, thereby ensuring optimal network performance. Furthermore, this solution is scalable for large networks and is adaptable to various network configurations, making it suitable for real-world applications. In contrast to existing solutions, our approach leverages built-in IEEE 802.11k/v standards to optimize network performance and operates autonomously. Additionally, this work marks one of the first practical applications of the IEEE 802.11k/v standard to address performance issues in real-world Wi-Fi networks. In summary, our method enhances network performance by operating within standard specifications and is suitable for large-scale deployment. To validate our results, we conducted multiple experiments, the details of which are documented in this research. To the best of our knowledge, this work contributes significantly to the knowledge in this domain by presenting a method to optimize home Wi-Fi networks using IEEE 802.16 standards. However, we discovered that using channel occupation metrics alone is insufficient to optimize network performance and thus we introduced the concept of AP/Extender selection to mitigate congestion. In addition, we identified performance bottlenecks in home routers and their devices, the details of which are presented in this research.
